item.title: Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap, provided their accounts are

The post Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap, provided their accounts are verified and they have weekly usage left.

Anthropic announced the change Friday as it renamed its two top consumer plans. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. They still cost $100 and $200 a month, respectively, and current subscribers don’t need to do anything to switch.

Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra.

Anthropic’s pricing page also lists monthly Claude Platform API credits: $100 with Max and $200 with Ultra. That adds another consideration for developers who use Claude Code while building applications against the API, with each plan bundling API credits equal to its monthly subscription price. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny highlighted the limit change in his own post.

What the five-hour cap meant

The five-hour limit capped usage within a rolling window, and a demanding task could burn through that allowance much sooner. Claude Code users could hit it midway through debugging or a large refactor and have to wait for a reset despite having weekly usage left.

Verification comes first

Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. The company says the checks help prevent fraud and abuse, and it will email users when the cap is lifted.

Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away.

According to Anthropic’, verification happens automatically based on account and payment history. There’s no way to request it or speed it up so some users will just have to be patient.

The weekly cap remains

Ultra users still have the same weekly allowance, and they could use it up sooner without the five-hour limit forcing them to pause. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max.

The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max.

Your chats with Claude count toward the same weekly limit as your Claude Code sessions, whether you’re on the web, desktop, or mobile. Once you use up that allowance, you can turn on usage credits to keep working at standard API rates, though you’ll pay extra on top of your subscription.

If you keep hitting the session limit with weekly usage to spare, avoiding those interruptions could make Ultra worth the extra $100 a month over Max, but if you already run out before the week is over, removing the session cap won’t give you more included usage.

OpenAI eases its limits

A day earlier, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux announced higher usage limits for Pro subscribers and Business Premium.

OpenAI also dropped a planned cut for existing $200 Pro subscribers after customers objected. In a separate pricing decision, the company abandoned an idea to replace token-based billing with flat per-job fees after developers pushed back.

Anthropic drops Claude’s five-hour session cap for verified Ultra users, so Claude Code sessions can run longer — but the weekly limit stays in place.

item.title: Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its

The post Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its first token quickly but take too long to finish an answer. It might respond promptly and still give the wrong answer. And a busy GPU tells the operations team little about either outcome. The operational challenge is connecting AI service behavior with the Kubernetes, GPU, compute, storage, and network conditions behind it—not viewing each layer in isolation.

That’s why you should measure an inference service before production, then compare live behavior with the baseline. In the fourth article in this HPE-sponsored series on AI and Kubernetes, The New Stack speaks with Marius Bogoevici, Senior Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software; Mahesh Ramachandran, Vice President of Product Management for HPE OpsRamp Software; and Karthik Subramanian, Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software.

Inference adds a further question: Does the whole service deliver a useful result at a cost and speed the business can support?

Earlier in this series:

  • Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.
  • Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap
  • Part 3: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.

Start with the experience, then establish a baseline

For a conversational service, Bogoevici recommends measuring time to first token, time per output token, reliability, capacity, resource efficiency, cost, and answer quality. The right mix depends on the experience a team intends to deliver. A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.

“A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.”

Time to first token and time to a complete response answer different questions. Inter-token latency and time per output token help explain generation speed after the first token arrives. Teams should document where they measure each interval and compare results under sustained load and demand spikes. Set targets for the particular workload and user experience.

Ramachandran urges teams to profile the AI serving system before customers depend on it. Test representative prompt and context lengths, output volumes, and traffic levels. Record token throughput, latency, and service-level measures under those conditions. The resulting baseline gives operators a reference to measure  production behavior changes.

Correlating those workload measures with infrastructure performance and capacity helps teams distinguish rising inference demand from resource contention and plan capacity more effectively. As Ramachandran tells The New Stack, teams should “profile it before you launch.”

Quality needs its own evaluation. Bogoevici says teams should ask whether the service gives proper answers or hallucinates. Platform telemetry can show a request was served, but data science and domain specialists need representative tests and acceptance criteria for the answer. 

The newly published ebook, Kubernetes in 2027: Building platforms for AI, autonomy, and scale, recommends assessing output quality alongside service performance and revisiting both after model, prompt, retrieval, or serving changes.

When the GPU is busy but the service is slow

GPU utilization is a useful signal, but it does not identify the bottleneck. Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.” That tells teams little about how the service actually performs. Ramachandran suggests checking whether inference pods scale on workload-appropriate metrics, whether requests reach the intended model, and whether related components can be scheduled when needed. Different models can have different latency and capacity demands, so a change in request mix can change the user experience even while GPU activity looks normal.

Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.”

Subramanian adds dependencies around the model: network configuration and database or vector-database response time. He raises another question: “Is the GPU partition too small to serve that model?” These are investigation paths, not a diagnosis that applies to every deployment. Teams should correlate them with the affected requests and time window before choosing a fix.

Kubernetes’ Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can use configured custom or external metrics, so teams do not have to replace it simply because CPU utilization is a poor trigger for inference. They do need to supply and test the metrics pipeline, scaling bounds, and available accelerator capacity for their serving stack. A scaling policy cannot make additional GPU capacity appear instantly.

What HPE Morpheus and OpsRamp contribute

HPE describes HPE Morpheus Software as a platform for governed provisioning and automation across hybrid environments. Its Advanced and Enterprise versions include HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS); Enterprise extends the operating model across hybrid and public-cloud environments. Platform teams can use catalog items, blueprints, access controls, and approvals to define how they request and manage supported environments. This gives platform teams a consistent way to deliver governed self-service and manage VMs and Kubernetes clusters together, reducing separate tooling and manual handoffs. Those capabilities alone do not benchmark a model or decide whether its answers are good.

HPE OpsRamp Software provides full-stack observability and monitoring across multi-vendor hybrid infrastructure and applications, with service maps, AI-powered event correlation, and operational automation to help teams understand dependencies and move from detection to resolution. Ramachandran describes HPE Morpheus as the provisioning engine and OpsRamp as the observability engine in HPE’s broader cloud operations approach.

Ramachandran says HPE’s combined solution includes Morpheus, OpsRamp and runtimes. He says it can measure token service rates in a model-serving environment and token request rates in an agentic workload. HPE is extending OpsRamp’s AI workload observability to connect model and agent activity, token volumes, token serving rates, inference latency, and time to first token with supporting infrastructure telemetry.

The operational value is the correlation: teams can investigate whether slow responses originate in the application, model-serving layer, or infrastructure, while using workload demand to inform capacity planning and cost accountability. For a specific deployment, teams should confirm which component emits each metric, how it is collected, and what additional application instrumentation is needed.

For agentic applications, HPE’s planned observability enhancements extend that context to AI traces, tool calls, errors, and quality signals alongside Kubernetes, CPU, GPU, memory, storage, and network telemetry. Lightweight eBPF and OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation are also planned to deepen visibility while minimizing collection overhead. These signals support investigation; they do not replace domain-specific answer evaluation or security controls.

As the preceding article in this series explains, collecting telemetry across a stack depends on deployed agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation. For an inference service, connect user-facing measurements with model-server metrics and traces, Kubernetes events, and relevant network, database, and accelerator signals. Check where visibility stops, especially at an external model or service boundary.

Plan for AI-specific routing and scheduling

Looking toward 2027, Ramachandran urges teams to examine autoscaling, model routing and scheduling as deliberate design choices for AI workloads. He discusses content-aware request routing, co-scheduling related components, and disaggregated serving. These are areas to evaluate for a specific architecture, not features that every Kubernetes installation or HPE product provides automatically.

An experimental Gateway API proposal describes pre-routing filters and cites the Inference Extension’s Body-Based Router as an example. That router can extract a model name from a request body for use in routing, but teams need a compatible implementation and configuration. They should measure any latency or efficiency benefit from routing and scheduling choices with their own models, traffic, and hardware.

Protect telemetry and share the launch decision

Inference observability also has a data-handling problem. Bogoevici warns that prompts, responses, and retrieved documents may appear in logs and traces. He asks, “What information is actually captured and where does it go?” Teams should decide what to collect, where to store it, how long to retain it, and who can see it. He stresses a simple point: prompts are data. Sensitive content needs protection even when teams collect it for troubleshooting.

Ramachandran sees operations and security observability moving closer together as AI agents introduce new events and access records. He says OpsRamp is preparing to interpret existing telemetry from a security perspective, while agent-specific activity may require additional instrumentation. Teams still need to design and test their security controls and incident response.

Before launch, Ramachandran recommends that business and IT stakeholders agree on the value the service should deliver, including a plausible inference volume tied to a business outcome. “There has to be measurable business value,” he says. 

“The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.”

Subramanian makes the sign-off point plainly: “It can’t be a single person.” Platform administrators, machine learning and data science teams, and security teams need to work together and plan for failures or attacks. Add the relevant business owner, test representative load and failure cases, and record the capacity, quality, cost, and recovery evidence behind the decision.

A launch decision should rest on evidence that the service can meet agreed user and business targets and that the responsible teams know what to measure and how to respond when it cannot. After launch, continue comparing AI workload behavior with infrastructure conditions so teams can detect regressions, troubleshoot across layers, and adjust capacity as demand changes. The goal is not simply busy GPUs, but reliable AI services with performance and resource use aligned to business needs.

The post Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes appeared first on The New Stack.
A healthy Kubernetes cluster and a busy GPU can still hide a slow or wrong AI answer. Profile inference before launch, then measure production against it.

item.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
item.dc:creator: Nick Lucchesi
item.description:
Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week,

The post What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week, replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work.

A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning.

“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.”

“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.”

Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools.

For Josh Bentley, SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding.

“People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said.

Darko Mesaroš, distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.”

“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally.”

“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said.

For Mark Cavage, Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents.

“The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said.

Cassidy Williams, GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating.

Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.”

The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs, head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC.

“Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said.

Frederic Branczyk, vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead.

“None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said.

The conversation is part of The New Stack’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together:

  • What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes.
  • What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what happens beyond the stage.
  • What tech industry experts enjoy most about developer events — Hallway conversations, old friends, and extended debates offer something a recorded session can’t.
  • Exciting releases for developers — Speakers share updates on agent tools, Git infrastructure, observability, and cloud sandboxes.
  • What tech leaders are focused on right now — Teams discuss agent development, engineering guardrails, infrastructure, and data privacy.

The post What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech? appeared first on The New Stack.
AI makes it easier to build software. Thomas Dohmke and other tech leaders explain what still worries them about learning, safety, and access.

item.title: Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams.
item.dc:creator: Bill Doerrfeld
item.description:
Welcome to the final edition of Road to KubeCon, where we track the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem each week on

The post Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the final edition of Road to KubeCon, where we track the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem each week on The New Stack as we head into KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, November 9-12 in Salt Lake City, Utah.

This week we explore how Kubernetes is getting new guidance for running AI workloads, including a new book from TNS, a dedicated Kubernetes working group, and advice on running LLMs across multiple GPUs.

Also in this day-before-Halloween-timed column, we’ve got OTel operators speaking a new language, security horrors from the latest AGNTCon + MCPCon, and untangling the dark webs of Kubernetes pod troubleshooting gone awry.

Join the conversation with HPE at KubeCon

HPE will have a big presence at KubeCon NA this year. The gold sponsor will be at Booths 151 and 145, where they’ll present live sessions throughout the day on topics spanning vSphere, HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS), distributed inference, setting up cloud storage for Kubernetes, and more.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.

This year, the focus is on gaining visibility and control across Kubernetes environments across VMs, infrastructure, and clouds. If you’d like to schedule a meeting with an HPE representative, contact jennifer.osuna@hpe.com.

TNS publishes Kubernetes guidebook for 2027 

In partnership with HPE, The New Stack has published a helpful book containing ten checks for teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes. The book, Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale, is available for download now.

Written by contributing writer Chris J. Preimesberger, the guide spans the full lifecycle, covering how to stress-test infrastructure before launch, how to meet the nuanced demands of agentic AI, what to watch for, and how to develop stronger permissioning models for agents.

Since agentic AI is prone to bursty, unpredictable behavior, arming your infrastructure with the right approach on Kubernetes is an important first step to production stability and success with AI at scale.

Kubernetes gets a Workload Conformance Working Group

Workload types have been expanding for years. And AI undoubtedly adds more variety. Against this backdrop, on Tuesday, October 27, the Kubernetes community announced a dedicated Workload Conformance Working Group.

According to Broadcom’s Nabarun Pal, writing on behalf of WG Workload Conformance on the Kubernetes blog, “The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes.” To do so, they’ll need community input, Pal adds. 

The Kubernetes AI Conformance test already determines whether a cluster can run AI or machine learning (ML) workloads. Yet none currently exists for workloads, requiring workarounds, manual exploration, or monitoring for signs like node drain or permission issues. So the new WG aims to create a similar standard for workloads.

It’s a significant step forward as the Kubernetes community grapples with a growing variety of workloads, including AI. Interested parties can read the working group proposal for more information, join the Slack channel, or attend biweekly meetings to get involved.

OpenTelemetry Transformation Language reaches v1

Earlier this week, the OpenTelemetry (OTel) project reached a milestone: the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) has reached v1. It’s stable for traces, metrics, and logs, and is included within Collector Contrib v0.164.0 and onward.

As Grafana Labs’ Tyler Helmuth recounts on the OTel blog, OTTL was created in 2022 as the configuration language for the transform processor. The domain-specific language lets you modify, filter, and enrich telemetry data directly at the collector level.

Longevity-thinkers will like this: They’ve also made a big backward-compatibility promise for OTTL. “If you write OTTL statements, the syntax and the standard functions stay backward compatible,” says Helmuth. 

As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.

Solving LLMs on shared GPUs

Putting all AI workloads on a single GPU is expensive and inefficient. But how do we pack multiple LLMs on shared GPUs safely, without a bunch of guesswork or manual toil? 

Ratnopam Chakrabarti, a senior solutions architect at AWS, took to X to share an early preview of his upcoming joint Nvidia–AWS session, which will seemingly answer this question for KubeCon attendees.

He says his KubeCon session will “demonstrate an agent pipeline that profiles workloads and handles model colocation on GPUs, all in real time.” It’s one of many KubeCon sessions this year tackling AI optimization on Kubernetes.

Troubleshooting GKE workloads with VPC Flow Logs

This week on the Google Cloud blog, Google Cloud product managers Nishant Kumar and Whitney Jenkins describe a common issue for cloud operators: Kubernetes pods are ephemeral, making them hard to troubleshoot.

As they describe, “In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols.” In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary; they add, and by the time you track them down, they’ve often already vanished — leaving little evidence or records to inform troubleshooting.

The workaround, at least for those using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), is its built-in VPC Flow Logs. This feature uses Google’s virtualized network to log every sampled flow with metadata like pod, workload, namespace, and service.

It’s one example of how cloud-native platforms are continuing to advance the infrastructure around Kubernetes to increase its visibility and usability.

AGNTCon + MCPCon prioritizes agent security

Is your agent installing malware without your knowledge? It’s a real possibility. 

The latest AGNTCon + MCPCon event this month in San Jose, California, featured plenty of interesting talks that might resonate with the cloud-native community looking at the agent trend with big, worried eyes.

For instance, Snyk’s Liran Tal gave a talk entitled Your AI Agent Installed Malware Because a SKILL.md Told It To. Tal covered how agents often get tricked into running malware and offered some guidance on how to prevent it.

Vstorm’s Antoni Kozelski and Bartosz Adam Gonczarek also presented how they built an e-commerce MCP server and let the agent experiment with purchases across four different hosts. It behaved drastically differently in each scenario.

The session opened a conversation about where authorization rules that allow or disallow agents from taking irreversible steps should live. For Vstorm, it meant placing them on the server, not locally. They’re also following up with a webinar on the subject soon.

These stories are just two examples of what we’re seeing a lot: the unintended consequences of giving AI agents the keys to the kingdom. Cloud-native operators should watch for stories like this as they build the foundational infrastructure to support agents.

See you at KubeCon

Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity.

And that’s a wrap for this year’s Road to KubeCon series! It’s been a privilege and an adventure profiling the top movements in the cloud-native world over the past two months.

In this weekly column, we covered many areas across eight editions, spanning updates to Kubernetes itself, like the Kubernetes 1.37 update and the move to cgroup v2.

Much of the discussion centered around how cloud-native technology is evolving for AI. We looked at case studies around Kubernetes inference at scale, and how agent harnesses are evolving.

Another recurring theme was increasing operator visibility. We saw how OpenTelemetry and Prometheus are converging and how to spot idle GPUs and optimize.

Arguably, the biggest takeaway is that the Kubernetes ecosystem is facing major shifts to meet the challenges of running AI workloads at scale. Is it up for the task?

KubeCon NA is anticipated to tackle this question head-on, from discussion at the co-located events to the main keynotes, sessions, and the showcase floor. 

View the Road to KubeCon archive for all editions in this series, along with other insights from the TNS and HPE teams. A big thank you to the column’s sponsor, HPE, for making this column possible, and to the community members who shared their insights.

Now, we’re excited to continue the conversation in person at KubeCon NA! 

See you there.

The post Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams. appeared first on The New Stack.
Kubernetes is drafting a runtime standard for workloads as AI adds more variety. Meanwhile, agent security horror stories show what’s at stake.

item.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at

The post GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at a tenth of its GPT-6 Astra flagship.

As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family, OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below. 

Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%. 

In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. This is a separate test of those trade-offs, not a replication of OpenAI’s computer-use benchmark.

The tests

I ran the final version of each test once per model through OpenAI’s API with reasoning effort set to high. I didn’t set an output-token cap, though the models still have built-in output limits. I graded each test against keys I built and verified, after developing three versions of each test. These are single-run results on synthetic tasks, not estimates of repeatability or performance across all workloads. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models. 

Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low.

Here is the final iteration of the tests. These are the tests detailed in the remainder of this article. In the usage figures below, “out” includes reasoning tokens; the parenthetical reasoning count is a subset, not an additional charge. Costs are estimates calculated from the reported tokens at standard uncached input and output rates, excluding any tool charges or billing adjustments. They are not verified invoice totals.

  • SQL reasoning – I built a fake database of 500 software builds and asked each model 25 questions about it. Some builds were deleted, some were retries, costs are in three currencies, and a few questions depend on time zones. Two of the questions can’t be answered from the data.
  • Data validation – I gave each model a spreadsheet of 4,950 fake customer records and 19 rules they’re supposed to follow. Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine.
  • Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage.

SQL reasoning

This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. For the questions that can’t be answered from the data, the correct answer was to identify that. On every other question, a model that didn’t give an answer earned zero.

Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was the total run time for 151 builds in a single region. Astra’s answer came in 406 seconds short of the correct 31,428. Its answer was 31,022 seconds, about 1.3% below the stated correct total. The final answer alone doesn’t show whether the error came from addition, a skipped row, or a misread value.

Astra was more accurate in this run, but its incorrect total still needed checking. It generated 27,970 reasoning tokens, and the response took 319.7 seconds—more than five minutes.

On the six questions that required adding up costs or durations across all 500 rows, Terra didn’t attempt an answer. It wrote a SQL query for me to run instead and marked each one as not calculated. Terra didn’t make up numbers, which is good. But it left the hardest part of the job, running the query and getting the totals, for you to do yourself. This is the first time I’ve seen AI hand work back.

The bigger problem is that Terra answered six questions wrong. Four of them were counts that were off by just one or two. Terra gave those answers with the same confidence as its correct ones, so nothing signaled that they were wrong. If you used those numbers in a report, you wouldn’t know which ones to double-check.

I’m including the numbers for both Terra and Astra here, but since the results were so different, the lower price and faster time aren’t wins.

  • Terra  133.1 s, 21,060 in, 11,554 out (10,707 reasoning), $0.079
  • Astra  319.7 s, 21,060 in, 28,806 out (27,970 reasoning), $1.65

Data validation

Astra scored a perfect 50, and Terra scored 45. 40 of the 50 points came from the 40 records that broke a rule. A model earned one point for each record it flagged, as long as it named the rule the record broke. The last 10 points came from records that looked wrong but followed every rule. A model lost a point for every correct record it accidentally flagged as incorrect.

Before giving its answer, Terra warned that it couldn’t reliably check all 4,950 records against the rules and might miss some (as it did in the SQL test). The reported input fit within the model’s context window, and I did not set an output cap. Terra generated 1,841 reasoning tokens compared with Astra’s 12,831. The responses took 31.4 and 145.0 seconds, respectively; these elapsed times don’t isolate reasoning time.

Terra correctly flagged 35 of the 40 invalid records and flagged none of the valid records: 87.5% recall and 100% precision in this run. Its 45/50 score is a test score, not an accuracy percentage across all 4,950 records. Three of the five it missed only break a rule when you compare them with other records in the file, such as a customer who reused another customer’s phone number. Terra flagged everything correctly, but it missed five invalid records. The results don’t explain why it missed them.

Astra caught all 40, but it took more than four times as long and cost about 12 times as much. Terra used fewer reasoning tokens and missed records in this run; that association does not establish the cause of the misses.

The numbers:

  • Terra  31.4 s, 234,045 in, 2,336 out (1,841 reasoning), $0.25
  • Astra  145.0 s, 234,045 in, 13,369 out (12,831 reasoning), $3.01

Incident log triage

This one was a tie, with both models scoring 50. I graded this test using a 50-point list of what a correct answer needs to include. To earn the full 50 points, a model had to trace the outage to the settings change in the ledger service, find the three servers with wrong clocks, and avoid blaming the planted false leads. False leads included a fraud service update that was rolled back, a payments setting that changed seconds before the real cause, a database switchover, and an unrelated memory problem in the search service.

Error messages blamed the fraud service, but both models traced the outage to a settings change in the ledger service and spotted the three servers with wrong clocks. Neither model took the error messages at face value. Both checked the evidence underneath, which is what you’d want from an engineer during a real outage.

Astra cost about 11 times as much as Terra and took 2.6 times as long to complete the work. Most of Astra’s additional output tokens were reasoning tokens: 4,628 of the 6,650-token difference. Both models earned the same score here despite that difference. These runs don’t show whether additional reasoning led to better scores on the other tests.

The numbers:

  • Terra  94.3 s, 251,651 in, 7,508 out (5,114 reasoning), $0.29
  • Astra  244.5 s, 251,651 in, 14,158 out (9,742 reasoning), $3.22

Results

I included GPT-5 Mini’s baseline results for reference. I rebuilt these tests several times and kept making them harder because both models kept returning identical scores. Because I selected these harder versions after seeing earlier results, they shouldn’t be treated as a representative sample of everyday work. A low Mini score is a comparison point, not an independent measure of test difficulty. 

What do I think?

In these three final high-effort runs, Terra generated fewer reasoning tokens and finished sooner than Astra. It scored lower on SQL reasoning and data validation, and tied Astra on incident log triage. That is a trade-off in the results, but it doesn’t tell us whether Terra was overwhelmed or why it made specific errors. 

The measured totals were 258.8 seconds for Terra and 709.2 seconds for Astra, so Astra took about 2.74 times as long overall. At the stated standard uncached rates, the estimated token costs were $0.61 and $7.88; Terra’s cost was about 7.8% of Astra’s. Terra scored 121/150 and Astra 148/150 under these test rubrics. The runs show a cost, time, and score trade-off; they don’t show that OpenAI deliberately cut reasoning to achieve it. 

Terra matched Astra’s scores on my earlier easy and medium versions, but that does not establish its accuracy on every task at those difficulty levels. On the final tests, I would be cautious about using it for unchecked numerical aggregation or exhaustive data validation. It may be an acceptable lower-cost alternative for some workloads, including tasks like the incident triage tested here, as long as you verify the results. Astra’s incorrect SQL total also reminds you to check its work. 

The post GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort appeared first on The New Stack.

OpenAI prices GPT-6.1 Terra at one-tenth of Astra’s standard input and output token rates. In these three tests at high reasoning effort, Terra used less time and cost less, but scored lower on two tests.

item.title: What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs
item.dc:creator: Doug Sillars
item.description:
P99 CONF is a virtual conference on high-performance, low-latency applications. Its 2026 event ran October 21–22. Here, we cover five

The post What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
P99 CONF is a virtual conference on high-performance, low-latency applications. Its 2026 event ran October 21–22. Here, we cover five of its 60-plus sessions. The recordings are available on demand at p99conf.io after registration.

Database storage design balances read amplification, write amplification, and space amplification (RUM conjecture). Improving one can increase another, depending on the workload and configuration. The five talks below show how engineers make those trade-offs across different database systems.

“Can Everything be an LSM?” 

Almog Gavra, Co-Founder at Responsive (now Databricks)

Gavra frames database design around read amplification (data read per result), write amplification (data written per logical write), and space amplification (storage used relative to live data). A log favors fast writes but makes reads work harder; a sorted array does the reverse. As Gavra put it, “I think about LSM trees as a mechanism for tuning between these two extremes.”

LSMs were built for local disks, but their immutable files also fit object storage. Gavra points to Amazon S3’s lower storage cost, durability, and availability, then names the trade-offs: objects must be replaced rather than edited, each GET and PUT has a price, and cold reads are slower. In his example, a local NVMe cache miss takes about 150 microseconds, versus 20–30 milliseconds for S3 Standard — roughly two orders of magnitude. LSMs batch writes into immutable files; caching helps keep object-store reads off the hot path.

Gavra’s SlateDB is an open-source, object-store-native LSM library. It exposes a key-value interface over stores such as S3, GCS, and R2, so developers can build data systems without implementing their own LSM.

How ScyllaDB Eliminates Read Amplification at Scale

Michael Litvak (Senior Software Engineer) and Felipe Cardeneti Mendes (Technical Director), ScyllaDB

ScyllaDB’s presentation examines Logstor, an opt-in storage engine for read-intensive key-value workloads, not a replacement for its existing LSM engine. For each key, an in-memory index stores a hash and the record’s location on flash. A read can return a cached value or find the record with one disk I/O, avoiding an LSM search across SSTables, Bloom Filters, and Indexed data structures. Tables using either engine can run in the same cluster with ScyllaDB’s existing drivers and consistency options.

The speakers’ preliminary read-dominant test sustained 1.1 million reads per second with p99.9 latency below one millisecond and p99.99 latency around 1.5 milliseconds. That test used 2 KB values; the earlier LSM examples in the talk used 1 KB values, so the results are not direct comparisons. They also reported similar throughput and sub-millisecond p99.9 latency in an 80% read, 20% write workload.

Logstor pays for those reads with a larger RAM index and more work on writes. Even a small update writes the full new value to a log, leaving the old record as dead space; segment compaction later reclaims it. The speaker positions it for bounded key sets, frequent overwrites, and point lookups where the extra memory is acceptable. During this talk, Mendes called the trade-off “optimized for time at the sacrifice of space.”

The Vertical Scaling Wall, and How Valkey Gets Over It

Madelyn Olson, Principal Software Engineer at AWS

Not every bottleneck is storage. Olson begins with Amazon ElastiCache customers who saw sudden p50 latency spikes, then tests where Valkey’s main execution thread reached its limit.

In Olson’s unpipelined GET benchmark, with about three million keys and 650 clients, p50 latency rose sharply near 150,000 requests per second. Valkey already had I/O threads, but they sat idle while the main thread executed commands. The team used lockless queues to keep network I/O and command parsing active on those threads while command execution stayed on the main thread. 

Olson reported a new ceiling of about 1.2 million requests per second in that workload — roughly eight times the earlier threshold. (This is the talk’s workload-specific result, rather than a general throughput guarantee.)

For horizontal scaling, Valkey 9.0 introduced atomic slot migration. The source shard keeps ownership while it streams a snapshot and subsequent changes to a target, then transfers ownership once the target catches up. Olson said a roughly 40 GB, three-to-four-shard test ran about 10 times faster without load and about five times faster under a heavy GET workload. If a migration fails before handoff, the staged transfer can be aborted without losing end-user data.

The I/O threads can be added or removed as workload demands change. Olson’s operating advice is to use horizontal scaling for baseline capacity and vertical scaling for short bursts, while keeping command execution single-threaded for now. Her guiding principle? “Efficiency trumps headline numbers.”

Searching 100B Vectors on Object Storage @ 200ms P99

Nathan VanBenschoten, Chief Architect at turbopuffer

VanBenschoten described turbopuffer’s search index at a scale of 100 billion vectors, representing more than 200 TiB of dense vector data. The company reports 200 ms p99 latency at more than 1,000 queries per second and 92% recall in early results. Object storage is the durable backing store, but this high-query-rate workload pins its data in local SSD caches. Hierarchical clustering groups nearby vectors; RaBitQ binary quantization shrinks a shadow index to one bit per dimension, allowing the search to narrow candidates before reranking a small subset using full-precision vectors.

The uncompressed search was limited by the bandwidth needed to move vectors from storage into memory. Quantization shifts more work into higher cache tiers, but it also increases arithmetic intensity, making the system CPU-bound. 

“Often when you push down one bottleneck, a new one emerges,” VanBenschoten said. That gives the team a different optimization target, including more efficient vector instructions.

To hold an index this large on SSDs, turbopuffer splits it across machines. VanBenschoten says its separated compute-and-storage architecture favors fewer, larger shards: a replacement machine can point to object storage and hydrate its local cache instead of receiving a full shard from another node. Queries fan out to the shards, and a coordinator combines their top results.

The Fastest Object Storage Client in the World*

Georg Kreuzmayr, Software Engineer at TigerBeetle

TigerBeetle is a financial transactions database. In this talk, Kreuzmayr describes the concept of “diagonal scaling”: keeping hot data on local NVMe while extending the storage hierarchy to shared object storage for colder data. 

A failed machine doesn’t need to reconstruct data already stored in object storage. As a scale illustration, he estimates that recovering 128 TB over a 100 Gbps network takes about three hours at line rate; if recovery takes longer than the interval between failures, a cluster can enter a failure spiral.

That design needs an object storage client compatible with TigerBeetle’s single-core transaction processing. Kreuzmayr cites the AWS C++ SDK’s blocking `getaddrinfo` call as one mismatch: A call on that core would stall transaction work. SDK thread pools, runtime allocation, and dependencies also conflicted with the project’s design goals.

TigerBeetle therefore built its own multi-cloud client rather than adapting the official SDKs. It supports S3, Azure, and GCP and can be tested with simulated I/O and injected faults.

Built in Zig, the client includes custom DNS, TLS, and HTTP components, uses `io_uring` and zero-copy sends, and allocates its working memory at startup. Kreuzmayr says the implementation is under 40,000 lines of code and has no dependencies beyond its toolchain. Those choices follow TigerStyle’s three principles: safety, performance, and developer experience.

In the talk’s S3 `PutObject` test — 8 MB requests over plain HTTP without checksums on an AWS `c7gn.metal-24xlarge` instance — Kreuzmayr reports uploads around 20 times faster than official SDKs and five times faster than a research implementation. For `GetObject`, he reports about three times the SDK throughput and roughly 25% more than the research implementation. He attributes the smaller download gain to the cloud TCP receive path. These are results for the stated test setup. The conference summarizes the broader client comparison as 4–10 times faster than official GCP and AWS SDKs.

Kreuzmayr’s takeaway is that building the client required more upfront work but made the code easier to test and tune. As he puts it, “code stops being technical debt and ends up being an asset.”

Performance is a process

Across the five talks, engineers identify different bottlenecks in storage, search, networking, and scaling. Their designs improve specific workloads while introducing new costs or complexity elsewhere.

Watch these and more than 200 other P99 CONF talks on demand at p99conf.io. Registration is required. P99 CONF is a ScyllaDB community.

The post What five P99 CONF talks reveal about database trade-offs appeared first on The New Stack.
Faster reads cost memory. Faster writes cost reads. Five P99 CONF talks show where engineers at ScyllaDB, AWS, and TigerBeetle chose to pay.

item.title: Sam Altman almost scrapped token pricing. Here’s why he backed off.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI considered dropping token-based pricing for its next model, letting developers submit a prompt and receive a price for the

The post Sam Altman almost scrapped token pricing. Here’s why he backed off. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI considered dropping token-based pricing for its next model, letting developers submit a prompt and receive a price for the work, before negative customer feedback convinced the company to back away from the idea, CEO Sam Altman says.

The flat-fee pricing idea

Speaking Thursday with Stripe President John Collison on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman recalls that OpenAI “almost made a very — what would’ve been a bad call” to stop pricing its next model in tokens altogether, moving instead to an arrangement where a developer hands over a prompt and OpenAI hands back a price.

The billing would have worked “like AWS,” he explained, where you “just do something and we send you a bill” rather than metering the exchange token by token. Altman does not name the model in question or give a timeline for when the change was under consideration.

We’ve cued up the exchange in the video below:

Why customers pushed back

The idea ran into resistance when OpenAI tried to gauge how customers felt about receiving a price with no breakdown. “The customer response on that is so negative,” Altman recounts, with buyers telling the company, “’I need to know what I’m paying for somehow.’”

“’I need to know what I’m paying for somehow.’”

Developers already spend plenty of time tracking input and output tokens to keep costs down and estimate what they’ll spend as usage grows. Getting a price without knowing how it was calculated would only make that harder.

Paying more for clarity

What makes the admission worth a second look is that, according to Altman, the people he consulted would rather pay more to keep that visibility. He put the question to “a few people,” asking whether they would take a higher rate for the same output as long as it stayed priced in consistent tokens, and the answer, he said, was that they would “much rather you inflate the tokens and pay more,” because “I know there’s a real thing there.”

“much rather you inflate the tokens and pay more … I know there’s a real thing there.”

Developers resist a single opaque price, he reasons, because they suspect that over the long run they are “gonna get screwed somehow,” the same instinct that once had buyers paying for CPU hours instead of for a finished job.

The proposal could have had significant implications for developers building agents, whose multistep workflows already consume unpredictable amounts of compute and make spending difficult to forecast even under today’s token-based model. Altman does not explain how OpenAI would have set those per-job prices, or whether customers could have weighed one charge against another.

Tokens, a ‘fake unit’

The subject came up when Collison pressed Altman on whether tokens were the right way to measure AI usage. Altman acknowledged the limitations of token pricing but had no clear alternative to offer.

“Tokens are a kind of fake unit … they’re real in some sense, but they’re not a good unit.”

“Tokens are a kind of fake unit,” he said. “I mean, they’re real in some sense, but they’re not a good unit.” He balked at Collison’s half-serious pitch to coin an intelligence-equivalent token, comparing it to the way chipmakers still market nanometer figures that no longer correspond to any physical measurement on the chip.

Altman admits developers incur real overhead when choosing between a cheaper model and a more capable one, especially when they also have to guess how much reasoning a given task will demand. “That’s just cognitive overhead that I don’t think actually adds any value,” he said.

The exchange comes as OpenAI continues to rely on token pricing, even as Altman has argued that the cost of a given level of AI falls roughly tenfold a year. For now, token pricing remains in place, even as Altman acknowledges its shortcomings and OpenAI struggles to find a better alternative.

Sam Altman says OpenAI nearly dropped token-based pricing for a flat per-job fee, but developers pushed back, wanting to know what they pay for.

item.title: AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes
item.dc:creator: Matthew Burns
item.description:
Earlier this month, the team behind Hydro developed a new way to check that a distributed system still works correctly

The post AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this month, the team behind Hydro developed a new way to check that a distributed system still works correctly when it resends messages after a failure.

This produced what Shadaj Laddad described to me as “like a 5000 line PR.” Hydro is an open-source Rust framework for distributed systems, the software that runs across many machines at once, and agents now write most of it with humans driving. The PR was difficult to split into smaller pieces as its components worked together. 

That’s a lot of code to review for a tool developers count on to catch bugs. Laddad, research lead for the Hydro team at AWS, says it’s something the team spends a lot of time thinking about. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose. He was set to give a keynote the next day where he was going to argue code review can’t keep pace with how agents write code.

Agents have let the team aim higher, Laddad told me, saying PRs arrive faster and run longer. “You can have the feature work well in isolation, then you mix it with something else, and suddenly the guarantees break down,” he said.

And you can’t just trust the tests. In most agent workflows, he says, the agent writes both the code and the unit tests. “Agents are great, but they’re unpredictable,” Laddad said. That unpredictability is part of what makes them creative, and it makes it hard for a human to review all those tests and confirm they do what the team wants.

His answer is shared Correctness checks outside the agent’s “zone of trust,” such as those enforced by a compiler. Rust’s borrow checker is his example: It catches race conditions before the code ever runs. Hydro does something similar for distributed systems, catching several types of bugs at compile time so an agent gets instant feedback on mistakes it introduced. The wider goal, which the team is still exploring, is domain-specific guardrails that agents can share.

To find candidates, the team studies historical projects for recurring patterns. Idempotency, ensuring a retried request doesn’t run twice, comes up repeatedly in design reviews, so the team is asking whether it can become a general-purpose guardrail. Laddad sees this as the next rung on an old ladder. C spared programmers from mangling function calls in assembly. Java took memory allocation off their plate. Agents, he argued, make the next layer more urgent.

Compilers have limits, though. As The New Stack reported in August, AI-generated Rust can compile perfectly and still be wrong.

The same team also built Infinity, an open-source agent runtime AWS announced on October 23. It suspends an agent while it waits on a tool call or a CI job instead of keeping it running. Laddad cited a benchmark showing 75,000 concurrent agents on a single Raspberry Pi. According to the AWS announcement, that figure is extrapolated from a server test in which each idle agent used about 100 KB.

Hydro itself is an early release, built for teams running high-throughput, low-latency services who are constantly worried about distributed systems bugs. Laddad noted that users should expect rough edges and a learning curve right now. The payoff is the confidence to change a system without fearing it will break a few months later.

Hydro and Infinity are open source at hydro.run, built jointly by AWS and UC Berkeley.

The post AWS’s Hydro team wants the compiler to catch coding agents’ mistakes appeared first on The New Stack.
Agents now drive most development of Hydro, an open-source Rust framework for distributed systems, producing larger pull requests at a faster pace.

item.title: Microsoft’s new Copilot harness makes agents easy — until you want to switch
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Microsoft is opening up the GitHub Copilot agent harness to outside developers through Microsoft Foundry, bringing the same orchestration infrastructure

The post Microsoft’s new Copilot harness makes agents easy — until you want to switch appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is opening up the GitHub Copilot agent harness to outside developers through Microsoft Foundry, bringing the same orchestration infrastructure used across its Copilot products into a managed service for building and deploying autonomous agents.

Announced Wednesday, the Microsoft Copilot harness is now available in public preview through Foundry Agent Service. It comes with built-in sandboxing, reusable skills, MCP integrations, and support for subagents. Microsoft takes care of running the agent and managing its execution environment, leaving developers to choose a supported model and configure the instructions and tools for their applications.

The same harness now supports Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, the CLI, and VS Code.

The company is also using GitHub’s agent infrastructure across more of its Copilot products. It’s a continuation of the Foundry strategy outlined at Build 2026, which focuses on making AI agents easier for companies to run, manage, and control. The same harness now supports Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot, the CLI, and VS Code.

Inside the managed Copilot harness

Microsoft’s harness manages model and tool calls, tracks context, and keeps agents within configured policies. Skills can package instructions, scripts, and supporting resources, while MCP integrations require authentication and approval. Agents can also work with files, run code, and delegate tasks to subagents, with the main agent coordinating the results.

Microsoft’s harness manages model and tool calls, tracks context, and keeps agents within configured policies.

How developers deploy agents

The company’s technical walkthrough shows how this works with a research agent. A Markdown-based skill lays out the steps for collecting evidence, analyzing data, and writing a report, while an azure.yaml file defines the model deployment, tools, instructions, and harness.

Developers select microsoft_copilot_preview as the harness type, deploy the agent using azd deploy --all and invoke it through the Azure Developer CLI. They can keep agent configurations and supporting files in source control, making it easier to track changes alongside their application code.

Runtime limits and lock-in

The Copilot harness must be selected when creating a prompt agent, and that choice can’t be changed later, even in a new version. Microsoft also controls how much CPU and memory the agent gets and how long it can sit idle. Developers can decide what their agents do, but have less control over the environment they run in.

Developers can decide what their agents do, but have less control over the environment they run in.

Microsoft is positioning its broader harness strategy as multi-model, although there are limits. Developers can choose from compatible models deployed through Foundry, but bringing their own models isn’t supported with the managed Copilot harness.

Teams that want more control can use Foundry’s hosted agents instead. Teams can build and run agents using their own frameworks and customize how they operate, while Microsoft handles the hosting. The company also announced general availability of long-running resilience for hosted agents on Wednesday, helping them recover from interruptions during tasks that take hours or even days to complete.

Foundry agent pricing explained

The Copilot harness in Foundry Agent Service for free until December 1, 2026, although model inference and some tools and connected services still come with separate charges.

After that, Microsoft will charge $0.0994 per vCPU-hour for compute and $0.0118 per GiB-hour for memory. Those rates may vary depending on the region and customer agreement.
