Microsoft is opening the GitHub Copilot agent harness to developers through Foundry, a managed runtime for building and running AI agents — with limits.

item.title: Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next
item.dc:creator: Matthew Burns
item.description:
Many MCP servers do just one thing. An agent asks for data and the server hands it back. AWS’s James

The post Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Many MCP servers do just one thing. An agent asks for data and the server hands it back. AWS’s James Ward thinks that leaves a lot on the table. The protocol works best, he told me, when the server acts less like a database and more like another voice in the conversation.

Ward is a principal developer advocate at AWS and sits on the technical committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, the Linux Foundation group that now houses MCP. I sat down with him last week at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose the day before he and co-presenter Alexander Ioffe were set to give a session on moving MCP from a basic API to an agent integration interface. 

“Many times our MCP servers are just these APIs, like ‘get me the customers,’ and that is a good place to start,” Ward said. “I imagine MCP as the third person in this conversation, or a fourth or a fifth, depending on how many MCP servers you have.”

In practice, that means a tool response carries guidance with the data. It tells the agent what it just did, what it might want to do next, and where to find more.

The other half of his pitch is visibility. Web developers can trace a click on a page all the way down to the database. “MCP by default doesn’t have any way to do trace ID,” Ward said.

The workaround AWS uses is rather low-tech. Add a session ID parameter to the tools and tell the agent to pass it on every call, so individual calls can be stitched into one journey. A second parameter can carry the user’s prompt or a summary of their goal. Teams can then compare what the user wanted with the path the agent took, build an eval around it, adjust a tool description or parameter, and measure whether more tasks get completed. Ward said AWS built much of this for the MCP servers its own developers use.

In May, AWS opened its MCP Server to everyone and added Lambda diagnostics in September. In an Agentic AI Foundation profile published before the conference, Ward described an agent fetching customer records one at a time because the server only offered a one-record tool. Watching the full journey is how teams spot that pattern and build a batch tool to fix it.

Ward didn’t present MCP as the only solution. AWS also ships a CLI and skills, he said, partly because MCP’s OAuth model can’t toggle between AWS user profiles the way the CLI can. Which works best depends on the model, the tool descriptions, and how the agent discovers tools, so AWS tests them against each other with evals.

None of this is exotic, and Ward knows it. “There’s nothing new under the sun,” he said. Observe the journey, reproduce it, measure it, and improve it. The difference is that teams now have to understand the path a human and an agent take together, and test whether changes to their tools actually help them finish the task.

The post Why MCP servers should tell agents what to do next appeared first on The New Stack.

Many MCP servers still behave like thin APIs that hand an agent raw data. James Ward, a developer advocate at AWS, argues they should guide the agent’s next move, and that teams need to see the agent’s whole journey to improve it.

item.title: Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: “There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors.”
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
On Thursday, Mistral released the weights for its frontier open model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), on Hugging Face.  Made available

The post Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: “There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors.” appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday, Mistral released the weights for its frontier open model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), on Hugging Face. 

Made available for preview just three weeks ago, the French AI company says ML4 has significantly improved since then, thanks to reinforcement learning and testing with customers and partners. Now, it claims, ML4 is the “best open agentic coding model in the world,” beating GLM-5.3 on cybersecurity and coding benchmarks (though only barely on the latter), at a fraction of the cost, Mistral says. 

“We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.”

From here, the AI company promises continued growth. In an embargoed press briefing attended by The New Stack, Pierre Stock, Mistral’s VP of Science, calls ML4 merely “a stepping stone,” saying, “We want to be in a position in which we dictate the frontier.”

Mistral’s VP of Science doesn’t want to live in a world without open weights

Stock told reporters that Mistral fully supports “the power of open weight,” calling it essential to ensure business continuity, transparency, and auditability for everyone: “I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said. 

“I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights [don’t] exist,” he said.

Recalling when OpenAI announced plans to cut off Cursor’s direct access to its models or when the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals, Stock’s case for open weights bears weight — perhaps why he says the philosophy is in the French company’s DNA.

“Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity.”

“Our stance is that AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor or an oligopoly can cut off electricity from one day to another.” 

Mistral puts open weights at the center of its approach. Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei has argued that open weights alone cannot resolve the concentration of AI power because access to computing infrastructure remains concentrated.

As Stock points out, this way, “nobody can switch it off because it can run either on your infrastructure or on an infrastructure that you can trust.”

Coding + cyber = the biggest impact

An open-weight model, though, does need the goods to back it up, and Mistral says ML4 is there, calling it “the best open model built in the West.”

To back those claims, the company points to Terminal-Bench 4.0, one component of Artificial Analysis’s Coding Agent Index, where, by Mistral’s numbers, Le Chonk — Mistral’s official nickname for ML4 — ranks as the top open model in the world for agentic coding, scoring 41% to Muse Spark Open’s 6%, Kimi K3’s 21%, and just eking past GLM 5.3’s 40%. 

“What the graph doesn’t tell you,” Stock said, “is that it’s more efficient than the competitors,” adding that Le Chonk uses 47% fewer tokens per task on average than GLM 5.3. “It means that you can get things done way faster and at a lower cost,” he explained.

Coding prowess, however, wasn’t the startup’s only focus when training its model. 

“We identified, really, coding and cyber as the two main areas that impact and that can benefit our customers and help them transform their entire business with AI,” Stock said in the briefing. 

So Mistral backed investments to advance the model’s cyber capabilities. In CyberGym E2E from the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which tests defensive cybersecurity capabilities, the French model once again pulls ahead of much of the competition, scoring 79% to GLM-5.3’s 29% (though Z.ai’s smaller GLM-5.3 Flash scored 74% in the same chart). In Mistral’s comparison, ML4 exceeded DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 1017’s 76% and tied MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s 79%.

To that point, Stock explains how some Mistral customers are already putting the model to work, using it to support automated pen testing, where specialized agents analyze an application’s logs and test for potential entry points. 

Breakneck improvements, at a fraction of the cost

When Mistral launched ML4 in public preview at the start of October, it came after about two months of training on about 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs in its European data centers. In the last three weeks, Stock says the model has undergone “significant improvement,” which he chalked up to the team’s reinforcement learning. Mistral’s own Terminal-Bench 4.0 score rose from 28% at preview to 41%.

“I have no information about someone being able to do it with this amount of resources.”

More notably, he claims, the French company ran that reinforcement learning on only 10 megawatts of power, “a fraction of what all the competitors have.”

When pressed on how Mistral can know with certainty that it’s more cost-efficient than its competitors, Stock told reporters, “I have no information about someone being able to do it with this amount of resources.” 

He also said Mistral’s resource efficiency means the French startup could advance further with the right investments: “If you give us 10 times more capital, then we’ll factor in these efficiency gains.” 

Mistral wants to lead the frontier

Throughout the embargoed briefing, Stock consistently referred to ML4 as “a stepping stone,” hinting at Mistral’s plans for what’s next. 

One certainty? Developers can expect smaller versions of Le Chonk to ship in the coming months, with Stock confirming, “There’s going to be a family of models, and one of them is going to be on a laptop.” 

Mistral says ML4 can help software engineers modernize legacy codebases (where OpenAI has recently made a striking leap for COBOL migration), as well as in finance, manufacturing, industrial engineering, and geospatial applications. Looking ahead, the French company seems to have its sights set on playing an even bigger role: 

“We think the only way forward [is] to own the entire stack.” 

The post Mistral’s Large 4 open weights arrive with a 1-point coding lead over GLM-5.3: “There’s nothing you can’t do with this model that you can do with competitors.” appeared first on The New Stack.
The French AI company calls Le Chonk “the best open agentic coding model in the world" — and says it is cheaper than anyone else.

item.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy
item.dc:creator: Sabari Sawant
item.description:
For more than a decade, the managed application platform industry has optimized around a compelling promise: get code running as

The post AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For more than a decade, the managed application platform industry has optimized around a compelling promise: get code running as quickly as possible. 

Five-minute deployments. Git-based workflows. Minimal configuration. Infrastructure abstracted away from developers. That simplicity changed how software gets built, and for good reason. Application teams should spend more time building software and less time assembling infrastructure. But for organizations in regulated industries, getting an application running is only the beginning.

A patient scheduling system, financial application, government service, or aerospace workload may remain in production for years. During that time, operating systems need patching. Runtimes reach end of support. Security requirements evolve. Applications scale. Teams change. Auditors ask for evidence. Regulatory frameworks expand.

For these organizations, the question is no longer simply: How quickly can we deploy? It is: How easily can we deploy, and keep that application secure, supported, observable, auditable, and operational for years?

“The services built for fast starts also need to support long stays.”

That is why platform selection for regulated workloads runs on three axes rather than one. Developer simplicity still matters. But compliance posture and service continuity decide whether that simplicity survives an audit or a roadmap change.

The missing middle in regulated industries

Large enterprises often address this challenge by building specialized organizations around their applications: platform engineering teams, SRE organizations, cloud centers of excellence, security engineering teams, FinOps practices, and dedicated compliance functions.

Many mid-size organizations operate under similar regulatory expectations without comparable specialization. A healthcare software company still needs to satisfy HIPAA requirements. A financial services company still operates within PCI DSS or SOX controls. Government contractors encounter FedRAMP requirements. 

Data residency, security reviews, vulnerability remediation, access controls, and audit evidence don’t disappear just because an organization has fewer engineers. Regulatory obligations do not scale down with the size of the engineering organization.

That creates a difficult operating equation. These teams need production-grade infrastructure and strong governance. But every hour their application developers spend maintaining deployment infrastructure, investigating platform issues, patching underlying systems, or reconciling configuration is an hour not spent improving the applications the business depends on. Workforce shortages in specialized IT roles compound the problem: the team keeping a patient scheduling application running is frequently the same team preparing audit evidence. This is not a question of technical maturity. It is an operating-model problem.

The applications already exist

Modernization discussions often begin with the destination: containers, cloud-native architectures, microservices, and increasingly sophisticated infrastructure platforms. Regulated organizations rarely have the luxury of beginning with a blank sheet of paper.

A mid-size healthcare organization might operate patient portal front-ends on Java and Tomcat, HL7 integration services on .NET and IIS, patient intake workflows in PHP, and lab data pipelines in Python. All in audit scope, all maintained by the same small team that also manages network security and prepares evidence for the next compliance review. Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient.

“Every organization has a modernization roadmap. Most are longer than the compliance calendar is patient.”

That creates an important test for any application platform intended for this market: Can it improve how organizations operate the applications they have today, not only the applications they hope to build tomorrow?

A Java Spring Boot application packaged as a JAR file should deploy without containerization, without a Dockerfile, without a container registry. A .NET Framework application running on IIS should deploy to Windows Server environments. 

That workload has no equivalent managed path on most modern platforms that focus exclusively on Linux containers. A Python service processing regulatory reports should deploy alongside a Java integration service in the same portfolio, managed through the same interface, with the same operational model applying to both. Modernization should not require transformation before organizations can realize operational benefits.

From an application problem to a portfolio problem

Managing one production application is an engineering problem. Managing dozens of independently operated applications becomes an operating-model problem. Consider an organization with 30 applications, each provisioned and managed independently. Each application brings its own deployment configuration, scaling model, monitoring setup, patching cadence, security controls, runtime lifecycle, and operational procedures.

For regulated organizations, that fragmentation carries another cost: evidence. Controls have to be understood. Exceptions have to be documented. Patching needs to be demonstrated. Security findings need to be remediated. Operational practices need to be defensible.

“Compliance programs rarely fail because of a single application. They fail because of drift.”

As the application portfolio grows, operational inconsistency becomes the largest source of complexity. The problem is not infrastructure cost. It is the multiplication of operational responsibility, and the enemy has a name: drift. Five applications deployed five different ways, each with its own conventions, gaps, and undocumented exceptions. Compliance programs rarely fail because of a single application. They fail because of drift.

The application platform therefore has a second job beyond making deployment easier: help create a repeatable operational model across applications, and make drift visible before it becomes an audit finding.

So what kind of platform addresses drift without removing the visibility regulated teams require?

Managed simplicity, visible control

The answer is not to hide infrastructure completely. For regulated workloads, abstraction without sufficient visibility creates a different problem. A service that abstracts infrastructure without providing audit visibility creates a compliance gap that no amount of developer experience can close.

The people accountable for the workload need to understand where it runs, how access is controlled, how networking is configured, how security policies apply, what gets patched, what changed, and what evidence is available to auditors. The more useful model is managed operational responsibility with appropriate customer visibility and control.

The application team provides its application and configuration. The platform automates the repetitive infrastructure work required to run it: provisioning, deployment, capacity management, load balancing, health monitoring, scaling, and platform maintenance. At the same time, the workload stays within the organization’s cloud environment, where its identity, networking, monitoring, security, and governance models still apply.

The right model delivers simplicity and account-level visibility, because the people accountable for the workload need both.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk has operated this model since 2011. A team provides application source code or a Dockerfile and configuration. The service orchestrates the AWS resources needed to run it: compute capacity, load balancing, auto-scaling, health monitoring, and deployment workflows. Environments run in the team’s own AWS account, not behind an opaque abstraction.

“A service that abstracts infrastructure without providing audit visibility creates a compliance gap that no amount of developer experience can close.”

That transparency distinction matters for compliance. Elastic Beanstalk is HIPAA-eligible and appears among AWS services in scope of SOC, PCI, ISO, and FedRAMP. Regulated industries ask about these frameworks by name. The claim is verifiable: organizations can download third-party audit reports through AWS Artifact and hand them directly to their own assessors.

From individual environments to a shared operational baseline

Over more than a decade of operating this model, AWS has spoken with more than 10,000 customers about how they build, deploy, and operate applications. Those conversations reinforced something important: customers were not asking us to choose between simplicity and production readiness. They wanted both. They wanted application developers to deploy without becoming infrastructure specialists. They wanted existing applications to benefit from managed operations without rewriting every workload first. 

They wanted AWS to take on more repetitive operational work while retaining the visibility, security boundaries, and controls their organizations require. And as their application portfolios grew, they wanted the operational model to grow with them.

The portfolio dimension matters most in this evolution. When each environment operates independently (its own deployment pipeline, scaling configuration, and patching schedule), the operational surface area grows linearly with the portfolio.

Elastic Beanstalk’s new Cluster Mode addresses this directly: multiple applications share managed infrastructure with a consistent operational baseline.

The implication for regulated teams is structural. The difference between twelve isolated environments and one shared operational baseline is not incremental cost savings. It reduces duplicated infrastructure controls, provides a consistent platform-maintenance model, and gives assessors one operational baseline to evaluate. Application code and dependency patching remain workload-specific. One operational model, applied across the portfolio, turns consistency from an aspiration into evidence an assessor can verify.

Production readiness is about time

What happens six months after deployment? What happens when a runtime reaches end of support? What happens when the security organization introduces a new requirement? What happens when an auditor asks for evidence? What happens when the organization grows from five applications to fifty? And what happens when the platform itself changes direction?

These are not edge cases for regulated industries. They are part of the expected lifecycle of production software. Among engineering leaders in healthcare, aerospace, defense, and finance, service continuity now ranks as the top evaluation criterion, ahead of developer experience and pricing. The industry spent a decade optimizing for developer onboarding speed. Regulated teams need platforms built for long-term operations.

The post AWS Elastic Beanstalk for regulated workloads: Built for the next decade, not just the first deploy appeared first on The New Stack.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk gives regulated organizations the visibility and compliance controls needed for long-term operational stability.

item.title: “I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub”: What GitHub’s leaders really think about their new rivals
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
At its annual Universe ’26 conference in San Francisco this week, GitHub took to the question of the platform’s stability

The post “I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub”: What GitHub’s leaders really think about their new rivals appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At its annual Universe ’26 conference in San Francisco this week, GitHub took to the question of the platform’s stability head-on.

The code-hosting company spent a significant part of the event’s keynote to talk about the investments it is making. That includes adding 4 million cores and 160 petabytes of storage, along with a full rearchitecting of its backend infrastructure.

But at a press conference and in interviews with The New Stack after the keynote, the leadership team of Jay Parikh, the executive VP of CoreAI at Microsoft who now leads GitHub, and GitHub COO Kyle Daigle also answered questions about what GitHub’s role is in this changing developer landscape — and how they feel about some of the competition that is now popping up in response to these changes.

It’s a timely question, since former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a GitHub alternative just a few days before GitHub’s conference.

When asked about Entire, Dohmke’s startup, at the press conference — and Microsoft’s M12 investment arm funding of Entire — Daigle diplomatically noted that Microsoft often invests in tools “that compete not only with GitHub but with the entirety of the Microsoft product estate. And that’s a good thing. That’s not a bad thing.”

Daigle noted that GitHub operates at a global scale, serves more than 225 million developers, and keeps iterating to better serve them.

“I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub.”
—GitHub COO Kyle Daigle

“I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub,” he said. “They might need different tools. That’s great, but what they need is [GitHub] to evolve for the agentic era, which is what we’re doing.

“The stats for the Git layer that we showed today kind of speak for themselves.”

Daigle stressed to The New Stack the role GitHub plays in the overall software development ecosystem — spanning individual developers, large open source projects, and Fortune 100 enterprises.

Daigle argued that the conversation about new Git forges, or version control forges more broadly, focuses too narrowly on companies and the economic use of those platforms. “I think that loses a core component of the problem,” he told The New Stack.

“We’ve never been the only Git host. We’ve never been the only SCM host,” Daigle said, pointing to Perforce and other options companies have relied on for years. What sets GitHub apart, he argued, is hosting all developers together at scale, rather than focusing only on enterprises or only on open source. “I don’t see folks trying to go solve that problem. They’re trying to solve a part of the problem,” he said. “There are places where they’re very opinionated and doing it in a unique way. I think that’s always been true.”

Daigle’s argument, at its core, is that it is much easier to build tools that focus on the enterprise. At least for now, that is where Entire and most other Git forges have their focus.

More sharply, Daigle said this moment “feels similar to the end of the zero interest rate era,” when “there were a lot of really talented, interesting developer tools, but they were just incredibly narrow.” He added: “Luckily, a lot of those folks ended up joining GitHub — and doing some really great work.”

“GitHub may not think there needs to be a new GitHub, but developers clearly do.”
—Entire CEO Thomas Dohmke

Entire’s reaction

When asked by The New Stack to comment on Daigle’s assessment that the world doesn’t need a new GitHub, Dohmke provided the following statement: “GitHub may not think there needs to be a new GitHub, but developers clearly do. Do we really want to put the future of software development and open source into the hands of a single big tech company? We are building Entire so the new home of the community is open source, scalable, and resident in many regions around the world.”

Platforms versus products

With new competition for users debuting in the form of Dohmke’s Entire platform, Parikh emphasized the importance of GitHub’s user community and the platform it offers at Wednesday’s press conference: “With how fast the world is changing around how we build and the lifecycle of software, the power of the community, I think, is more important than it’s ever been in terms of what we’re creating, how we’re sharing, how we’re learning together.”

Parikh made a similar point in a later interview with The New Stack, drawing a distinction between individual development tools and the platform that supports them when asked about the competitive landscape GitHub now faces.

“GitHub and Microsoft have always been platform companies,” he said. “So much of what’s out there are products, and yes, we have products, and we have platforms.”

For Parikh, that means offering a complete development workflow while also letting developers choose which pieces they use. Or as Daigle put it, “we’ll give you the full flow, or we’ll give you the primitives, which I think is what most companies want. Everyone’s interested in what is the one way to do this, but nobody wants to buy the only way. They want to have the optionality and the choice.”

Where agents break things

Supporting those varied workflows ended up forcing GitHub to reconsider some of the assumptions the team had made about which services were most likely to fail.

“The places that have failed are not the places we would have expected to fail historically, because agents act in such a different way than a human being,” Daigle said. “Some services that were scaling perfectly, and we thought were good to go for quite some time, had a surprising failure.”

Those failures began emerging in early summer, prompting GitHub to look beyond adding capacity as the main solution.

“It’s not just increasing the number of cores, the overall horizontal scaling, but looking at core services that need to be completely rewritten because the behavior pattern is so incredibly different,” Daigle said.

Parikh, whose experience includes scaling infrastructure at Facebook and Akamai, said the current growth rate makes incremental improvements pointless.

“You have to take a full systems look at it,” he said. “Getting five or 10% here or there, it lasts you two weeks or a week now.”

What makes all of this harder is that GitHub has to make those changes while keeping the service running and compatible with existing workflows. And in the meantime, the traffic patterns are changing, too, Parikh said.

“The traffic patterns are also not static right now … We optimized CPU, and now all of a sudden the bottleneck is going to move somewhere, and then you’re like, ‘Oh, I thought it would show up here, but it showed up here.’ Right now, the good news is you do these in staged rollouts. You test these things, and then you adjust,” he said.

One substantial architectural change the team has committed to is separating compute from storage in GitHub’s Git infrastructure. This now allows the company to more easily scale each according to demand.

“Depending on what that traffic is, time of day, who’s using it and what type of product offering sits on top of it, you can scale these things independently and optimize for how that compute workload changes and how that storage workload changes,” Parikh said at the press conference.

Moving from GitHub’s own data centers to Azure also provides more capacity, geographic flexibility and redundancy, Parikh said, which the existing facilities could not offer. But he also stressed that the work remains unfinished and includes additional changes to harden and scale GitHub Actions, for example.

“We can’t add the capacity. We don’t have the scale in those fixed data centers that GitHub has operated on, and so moving into cloud infrastructure that gives us flexibility and scale and location and redundancy and network and all that is much better for us,” Parikh told The New Stack.

Keeping free repos free

Interestingly, these architecture changes also affect the economics of hosting all open-source code and free repositories on GitHub.

Daigle said that separating compute and storage should reduce the cost of storing Git repositories, helping GitHub maintain access as developers and their agents create more work.

Daigle said GitHub has a responsibility to its community. Suddenly limiting developers to a handful of private repositories “breaks the whole contract of what GitHub is,” he said.

Daigle said anyone writing code, whether they’ve done it for years or are just starting, should have a home on GitHub. “A repo should not be hidden out on your laptop, or [be] an HTML file shared between friends,” he said. “We have a place for that.”

He did, however, distinguish that commitment from the cost of supplying AI models. GitHub cannot give everyone unlimited free tokens, he said, and has had to decide where to subsidize access.

Rethinking Git and verification

Beyond GitHub’s own infrastructure, Daigle also sees room to change Git itself. He wants the company to work with the community on its underpinnings and sees a role for something like “a porcelain layer on top of Git,” which he described as a higher-level interface that simplifies access to the underlying system.

Daigle said GitHub needs to “assert our role in the community” and work with established and new players alike to rethink some of Git’s underpinnings. “They kind of didn’t make sense before the agent change,” he said, “and now they really, really don’t make sense.”

At the same time, though, Daigle remains cautious about whether this agentic era needs an entirely different version control system.

“I want to know we need to move before we move,” he said. “I don’t think we’re done with [Git] yet. I just think we do need to lean in more.”

“You actually need to review it, you need to push it into production, you need to run other workflows, you need to do AI scanning for security issues,” Parikh said at the press conference.

Daigle expects verification — reviewing, testing, and deciding whether software should reach production — to become the next bottleneck.

Daigle expects verification — reviewing, testing, and deciding whether software should reach production — to become the next bottleneck. He argued that even unlimited CPUs wouldn’t make running every build after every agent commit desirable.

“If I have 5 or 10 agents running at a single time, I don’t actually want or need all those builds for the sake of the agent,” he said. “And that requires a change in behavior for the agents or the humans involved.”

Among the possibilities he raised were signing locally executed builds and submitting them with an agent’s work, selecting a smaller set of relevant tests, and exploring proof-driven development. The right combination of tests, evaluations and live verification will depend on the application.

“If you’re an automaker, you’re not going to say, ‘Well, I’ll let my agent check if the brake caliper was engaged or not,’” he said.

The post “I don’t think the world needs a new GitHub”: What GitHub’s leaders really think about their new rivals appeared first on The New Stack.
GitHub is rebuilding its backend for AI agents. Its leaders tell The New Stack what broke, how free repos stay free, and why the world doesn't need a new GitHub.

item.title: Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share
item.dc:creator: Adam Crowder
item.description:
Ask a platform team what they built last year, and the list likely includes a Kubernetes controller that creates a

The post Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a platform team what they built last year, and the list likely includes a Kubernetes controller that creates a few objects in order and copies fields between them. No business logic, just wiring. A Deployment, a Service in front of it, and a ConfigMap whose one interesting value is the hostname the Service reports in its status. Kubebuilder turns building the first controller into a pleasant afternoon. The tenth brings its own reconcile bugs, upgrade path, and on-call rotation. It’s the same controller. It’s slightly different each time, and it exists in thousands of organizations.

Every ingredient, no recipe

Kubernetes has the ingredients: CRDs define new types. Controllers give them behavior. Server-side apply tracks who owns each field. CEL evaluates expressions, and OpenAPI schemas type every field. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it.

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!

Every tool that manages a set of resources builds that piece itself, and keeps adding to it. Helm does it at render time, and Helm 4 added server-side apply and waiting on resource status. Argo CD has sync waves, hooks, and health checks because manifests cannot say what order they need or when they are done. Crossplane has compositions and functions, and v2 composes native Kubernetes resources directly. Operators do it in Go, by hand. Strip them down and the kernel is the same: a set of objects, dependencies between them, values flowing along the edges, and something that keeps re-checking whether the cluster still matches. Each recent addition reaches for a part the tool lacked: order, readiness, per-field ownership, evaluation inside the cluster.

“Kubernetes has the ingredients. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it.”

If everyone is building the same piece, the question is whether it should be shared. That is the position of kro, the Kube Resource Orchestrator, and why it moved to Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider in September 2025 as a primitive that other things build on, not another end-to-end platform.

Taking the controller apart

Kro started by taking the hand-written controller apart. API mechanics and lifecycle are the same in every one; only the wiring differs. Its answer, the ResourceGraphDefinition, writes the wiring down as data, and one controller interprets every definition. CRDs, OpenAPI, CEL, and server-side apply were already there, and kro connects them.

A ResourceGraphDefinition holds two separable things:

  1. The composition (the template with resources behind each instance and the CEL expressions to reference between them)
  2. The API (a schema, the CRD generated from it, and the instances application teams create)

The composition

kro derives the dependency graph from the references in CEL expressions (so order is never explicitly declared) and type-checks every expression against OpenAPI before an instance exists. The opening example’s ConfigMap needs the Service’s hostname, so its template names that field. That reference is the entire ordering rule: the ConfigMap reads from the Service, so the Service comes first, and nobody writes the order down. An explicitly declared order is a second description of a relationship the manifests already contain, and the two can disagree after any rename or reorder. An inferred order cannot drift, because it is derived rather than defined separately. The dependency is the reference. Wherever order is declared apart from the reference that needs it, there are two sources of truth, and an opportunity for drift.

The API

A platform team writes the ResourceGraphDefinition and application teams get a Kubernetes API like any other, with kubectl, RBAC, and GitOps working as usual. Ten glue controllers become ten definitions run by one controller. Wiring as data makes an API cheap to create, and a cheap API is still a promise. Application teams point manifests, RBAC, and pipelines at it, and from then on a removed field breaks something the platform team cannot see. kro refuses a ResourceGraphDefinition schema change that would break existing instances unless the author explicitly allows it. The cost of an abstraction moved from writing it to owning it: ten codebases gone, ten APIs left. Teams should count APIs, not controllers.

The primitive on its own

Once composition became cheap, people found more use-cases, and not all of it needed its own dedicated API. A default-deny NetworkPolicy in every labeled Namespace. Labeled Services folded into one Ingress. A DNS stack installed once and kept healthy. Nothing directly requests these; they react to what is already in the cluster. They are one-off definitions that do not need a repeatable API.

kro 0.10 adds a primitive for this case. A Graph is the composition piece alone; namespaced, with no schema, no CRD, and no instances. The Ingress case, abbreviated:

apiVersion: kro.run/v1alpha1
kind: Graph
spec:
  nodes:
    - id: services
      ref:                          # read only, never owned
        kind: Service
        metadata:
          selector: {matchLabels: {expose: "true"}}
    - id: ingress
      template:                     # created and owned
        kind: Ingress
        spec:
          rules: >-
            ${services.map(svc, {"host": svc.metadata.name + ".example.com", ...})}

Nobody creates an instance. The Services already exist, and the Graph follows them: label one and a rule appears; remove the label, and it goes.

Of the two halves, only one was ever new. The API half is a CRD, which is a primitive Kubernetes already has. ResourceGraphDefinitions make them cheaper to write, but the primitive was already there. The composition half is the piece Kubernetes lacked and every tool built for itself. Graph is that half on its own, and standing alone it shows what was easy to miss before: the API was never the input, only one kind of input. A composition reconciles against cluster state, and a new instance of a custom resource is just one of the many changes to that state it can react to. Whatever the change, the work is the kernel from earlier: objects, references between them, and a continuous declarative reconciliation loop keeping them in sync. That is the primitive. A ResourceGraphDefinition is the same primitive with a CRD in front of it.

“Strip the trigger from anything that creates objects, copies values between them, and keeps checking, and what is left is a composition.”

The split travels. Strip the trigger from anything that creates objects, copies values between them, and keeps checking, and what is left is a composition. An operator serving one custom resource is a composition with an API in front. A pipeline stage that applies manifests in order and waits for them is a composition with a commit in front, minus the loop. A runbook that creates a Namespace, its quotas, and its role bindings is a composition with a ticket in front. Seen that way, the question is no longer which tool to adopt but where composition is already happening and what is doing it.

Graphs in disguise

Kubernetes platforms are already full of resource graphs; they just aren’t written down as such. A naming convention so two manifests agree on a string. Sync waves or hooks that encode a dependency graph as step order. A script that copies a status field into another object. Each exists because the tool underneath cannot express a dependency between two objects, or cannot see what the cluster holds right now, so the dependency lives somewhere else such as a string, a step number, or a script. A composition tool puts it back as a reference between the objects. In kro that reference is a CEL expression continuously watched and evaluated inside a graph.

A familiar move

Kubernetes has grown this way before. Rolling updates were a kubectl subcommand until the Deployment controller took them over, and everything above got simpler. Composition looks due for the same move. kro, a Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider subproject on GitHub, shows what changes when the composition machinery becomes reusable, and the relationships become declarative. The question is bigger than any one project: if composition is what nearly every platform needs, should every platform have to build it for itself? Composition may be the primitive Kubernetes is missing.

The post Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share appeared first on The New Stack.
Stop rebuilding glue controllers. Learn how declarative resource composition provides the missing orchestration primitive Kubernetes needs.

item.title: The 5 essential layers of AI agent sandboxing on Kubernetes
item.dc:creator: Mickey Boxell
item.description:
An AI agent given autonomy to run code will inevitably run code no human has reviewed. It may install model-selected

The post The 5 essential layers of AI agent sandboxing on Kubernetes appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An AI agent given autonomy to run code will inevitably run code no human has reviewed. It may install model-selected packages, run scripts generated moments earlier, and iterate until a developer’s test passes; that risk is limited to a laptop. For a company, it can extend beyond the agent’s workload to any workload deployed on shared Kubernetes infrastructure. Cluster configurations can limit a container’s system calls, but an allowed call that reaches a kernel vulnerability can still expose the underlying node.

As agents proliferate, this gap has shifted workload isolation from a niche hardening requirement to a baseline need for platforms that run agents. This is a challenge our users at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) have asked us to help solve.

KubeCon + CloudNativeCon takes place in Salt Lake City, Utah, from November 9 to 12. Register now.

As expected in the cloud-native space, the community has developed solutions. These solutions exist across five layers: from the pod request, down to the node, and back up to the agent’s session. Platform teams can assemble the stack rather than reinvent it, while native provider support simplifies configuration and maintenance. Managed Kubernetes services offer sandboxed pods this way, but runtimes isolate agentic workloads differently.

The following sections cover the options and tradeoffs before showing how the components fit together.

1. The isolation layer: choosing your risk boundary

First choose between minimal isolation, a restricted kernel interface, and full VM isolation. Each option comes with trade-offs between security and performance.

runc offers the greatest performance through a shared host kernel. Seccomp-based filtering restricts the system calls a process can make.

gVisor suits use cases where a restricted kernel interface is sufficient. Its user-space application kernel handles system calls instead of booting a guest Linux kernel, so the workload reaches the host through a small interface. gVisor implements a subset of Linux, so it starts quickly and packs densely. Applications must work with the interfaces Sentry implements, which can constrain agent behavior.

“A separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents.”

Kata Containers suit use cases requiring full VM isolation. Each pod runs in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, at the cost of a VM boot and guest-kernel memory. Nearly anything that runs in a container runs in Kata. Agents exercise package managers, compilers, nested builds, and headless browsers. For that code, a separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents.

2. The node: assembling it and accounting for it

Worker nodes must be configured for the selected sandboxed runtime.

runc containers use Linux namespaces to separate process, filesystem, and network views, and cgroups to control resource use. They share the host kernel. Nodes need runc configured through a runtime such as containerd, but no guest kernel or hypervisor.

gVisor handles workload system calls in Sentry, while a separate Gofer process mediates access to host-backed files. Each eligible node needs the gVisor runtime installed and integrated with containerd.

Kata Containers place each pod in a lightweight VM. Workload system calls go to the guest Linux kernel, separated from the host by hardware-backed virtualization. This adds overhead and requires bare-metal nodes or VMs that support nested virtualization. In aKernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) setup, nodes need the Kata runtime shim, a supported virtual machine monitor (VMM), KVM and hardware virtualization, plus a guest kernel and image containing the kata-agent. You must maintain that guest image. A kernel CVE means patching two kernels. For use cases requiring flexibility and strict isolation, that burden may be necessary.

3. The access layer: limiting the agent’s reach

A sandbox protects the host from the agent, not from anything it’s handed. Code inside can still delete a writable repository, read a mounted secret, or send data wherever the network allows. Sandbox policy matters as much as the sandbox itself:

  • Network: Default-deny egress with a NetworkPolicy, then allow only the destinations a task needs, such as a package mirror or model endpoint.
  • Credentials: Issue short-lived credentials scoped to the task, not long-lived tokens mounted into the pod. A leaked credential expires with the task.
  • Storage: Mount repositories and data read-only unless the task needs to write, and give writable workspaces their own volume.
  • Remote tools: Give API endpoints and MCP servers their own authorization. They run outside the sandbox, so its boundary does not cover them.

4. The request: RuntimeClass

Kubernetes lets users retain the standard Pod API while selected pods, including agents, opt into a more isolated runtime. RuntimeClass lets pods select the security and performance balance they need without taxing non-agentic workloads.

Additional isolation affects resource consumption and pod readiness. gVisor’s Sentry processes and Kata’s guest kernel, kata-agent, and VMM add memory and CPU overhead. Add measured overhead to the RuntimeClass so the Kubernetes scheduler and resource quotas account for it. Measure your workloads rather than copying an example.

Cluster administrators create a RuntimeClass matching the node’s configured runtime. It tells Kubernetes the runtime is available, how pods select it, and what overhead it needs:

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata              # runtime name in the node's containerd config
overhead:
  podFixed:
    memory: "160Mi"        # example value; measure your own
    cpu: "250m"
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    sandbox.example.com/kata: "true"
A pod opts in through the runtimeClassName field of its spec: 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: agent-task
spec:
  runtimeClassName: kata   # or gvisor; omit for the default runc
  containers:
  - name: workspace
    image: python:3.12

Everything else stays the same. Workloads that do not need sandboxing omit the field and use the default runtime. A cluster can expose each runtime as a separate RuntimeClass.

5. The session layer: Agent Sandbox

Agent work comes in bursts. An agent runs code, then waits minutes or hours for the next interaction with a model or human. Keeping a VM running keeps it ready to resume work but consumes capacity. Tearing it down saves capacity but requires rebuilding it later. Warm pools offer a middle ground, but reserve capacity.

“Agent work comes in bursts. An agent runs code, then waits minutes or hours for the next interaction with a model or human.”

The Agent Sandbox project, owned by Kubernetes SIG Apps, standardizes this choice. Its Sandbox API creates stateful single-pod environments with stable identities and persistent storage, plus extensions for templates, claims, and warm pools. It remains runtime-agnostic and leaves isolation to the selected RuntimeClass.

Our approach: building on community projects

Community projects have helped us achieve our goal of letting users run untrusted agent code on shared infrastructure using Kubernetes tools they already know. They keep workloads portable: the same pod spec runs on any conformant cluster. Security fixes and design reviews come from a network larger than any one vendor. And frameworks that integrate with Agent Sandbox do not need a new API. Thanks to the community, users can adopt these new tools without reinventing the wheel. 

We are thankful to be a part of this dynamic space and excited to see it evolve.

Discover the five essential layers for sandboxing autonomous AI agent workloads securely on shared Kubernetes infrastructure.

item.title: “Urgency is an inherently subjective call”: Anthropic tells TNS how it grades Claude Duet
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic built Claude Duet, an AI assistant that monitors your connected apps and works on tasks in the background, to

The post “Urgency is an inherently subjective call”: Anthropic tells TNS how it grades Claude Duet appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic built Claude Duet, an AI assistant that monitors your connected apps and works on tasks in the background, to decide what needs your attention without being asked. A week after its October 21 debut, the frontier lab with an IPO in its sights has shared with The New Stack how it is testing whether Duet gets those priorities right.

Anthropic has developed internal graders to assess how Duet prioritizes tasks, though urgency can be subjective. The stakes rise when an agent manages work across email, calendars, and B2B apps. Duet can remain within its permissions and still get its priorities wrong.

Powered by Claude Opus 5.5, Duet can prepare work and flag items it thinks need attention without waiting for instructions. Anthropic has been testing that approach with its own employees, using their day-to-day work to see how Duet handles competing priorities.

Testing Duet’s judgment

“After using Duet for our day-to-day work at Anthropic, we calibrated graders that assess correctness in task prioritization, and we run them offline against cases representative of internal use and early external testing,” a company representative tells The New Stack.

Those graders measure whether Duet can distinguish what deserves attention from what can wait, though Anthropic acknowledges the difficulty of evaluating those decisions.

“Urgency is an inherently subjective call, so we found building an eval for it imperfect but quite helpful,” a company representative says.

Duet can spot tasks like an approaching deadline or an email requiring a reply, but it doesn’t always know which task should be a priority, and the company admits the agent can misread conversations or misjudge urgency. Anthropic’s public launch and support materials do not say how often that happens.

Testing Duet’s safeguards

On October 23, two days after Duet’s debut, Anthropic published a closer look at its safety, privacy, and security safeguards. Duet team lead Karan Ahuja pointed to the post while addressing feedback received through messages, emails, and public posts.

Anthropic keeps the part of Duet that does the work separate from the part that checks whether the work matches what the user actually asked for.

“A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code and extended for Claude Duet,” the rep tells The New Stack. “It assesses whether the action matches your intent.”

Because that check runs independently of the model performing the task, Anthropic says instructions hidden in a webpage can’t directly steer the classifier’s decision.

Anthropic says an outside firm penetration-tested Duet, but its public materials don’t show how reliably the separate check catches actions outside the user’s intent. Related research illustrates the difficulty of enforcing this agent scope: Researchers found that removing a prompt section defining authorized and out-of-scope actions in Claude Code tests increased out-of-scope actions, although that study did not test Duet’s separate classifier.

Limiting prompt injection

The separation is designed to reduce prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded in emails, documents, or webpages try to redirect an agent. Researchers have already explored this risk by leaving hidden messages for rogue agents and observing how they responded. Anthropic’s support materials still tell users to review drafts and approval requests because Duet may encounter prompt injection.

Duet uses the apps already connected to a user’s Claude account. Disconnecting an app stops new access, but information Duet has already stored in memory remains until the user resets it. Anthropic says Duet never sees passwords, browser cookies, or sign-in tokens, and can’t save them to memory.

Duet is designed to seek approval before actions such as making payments or deleting items. Sharing private health or financial information requires consent, though an explicit request to share it can count as that consent, while trading securities, moving money between bank accounts, and accessing someone else’s account remain off-limits entirely.

Summaries, not surveillance

Users can see what Duet has finished and what’s still underway through its task list, with a separate page for each job. They can also give the agent new instructions while it’s working.

But users can’t see everything happening behind the scenes. During the research preview, users can’t watch Duet work in its cloud browser or take over the browser. Users can review its task activity and approve actions, but they can’t inspect each browser step as it happens. (The public launch and support materials do not describe a way to undo completed actions across connected apps.)

What background work costs

Duet uses the same allowance as regular Claude conversations, so background work counts against a subscriber’s plan limits. How much it uses depends on the job.

“Larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, will require more model turns and background work,” the Anthropic rep tells The New Stack.

Even Duet’s routine checks across connected apps count toward the five-hour session and weekly limits.

Those checks happen every few hours rather than continuously, partly to avoid using up a subscriber’s allowance. The downside is that something urgent could arrive between checks and go unnoticed until the next one. Checking more often would use more resources, while checking less often could leave users waiting longer for an alert. (Anthropic’s public launch and support materials do not quantify how much of a typical subscriber’s usage goes toward background activity.)

Duet’s research preview is available by waitlist to U.S. Pro and Max subscribers. Anthropic employees have used it to work through to-do lists while they’re away and talk through workloads on walks, though Anthropic admits the agent isn’t as reliable with consumer tasks like booking tickets.

The company expects to keep adjusting the product as testing continues.

Anthropic’s Claude Duet is an AI agent that decides what needs your attention. Here’s how it tests its judgment — and where it still falls short.

item.title: Google just handed its rivals the keys to Android
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google is giving coding agents like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex deeper access to its Android development tools, including

The post Google just handed its rivals the keys to Android appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google is giving coding agents like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex deeper access to its Android development tools, including devices, performance profilers and production crash reports; now, agents can now investigate bugs, test changes, and verify their own fixes.

The push spans Android Studio and the terminal-based Android CLI, with Google opening both to third-party agents rather than steering developers toward Gemini. Matthew McCullough, vice president of product for Android, has emphasized giving developers the freedom to choose their own models and coding agents.

In a Wednesday post, Adarsh Fernando, senior product manager for Android developer tools, describes the goal as giving developers and their agents “the tools and knowledge to build high-quality Android apps faster.” The updates were announced Wednesday at Android Dev Summit.

Bring your own agent

The company’s Bring Your Own Agent feature now supports more than 40 coding agents that speak the open Agent Client Protocol, among them Anthropic’s Claude Agent, OpenAI’s Codex, and Google’s own Antigravity, and Google says the feature is now stable in Wednesday’s release of Android Studio Rabbit 2.

A developer can install several and switch between them without leaving the IDE, and connected agents inherit the IDE’s own read on a project — its structure, build configuration, symbols, and tools such as Compose Preview, the emulator, and Logcat — context they would otherwise have to rebuild through code searches and terminal guesswork.

Alongside it, a new Change Review feature scans an agent’s pending changes for common issues and can walk a developer through a large set of modifications before anything is applied, and Google is pushing the same reach beyond the IDE with official Android CLI plugins for Claude Code, and Codex that cover project creation, emulator management, UI inspection, and its Android documentation.

Compose previews from the terminal

Another announcement includes the new android preview command that lets coding agents render Jetpack Compose previews directly in the terminal without launching an IDE or emulator.

The company says agents using it completed UI tasks 77% faster while using up to three times fewer tokens, though it shared little about how it measured those results. The CLI also adds android device remote, giving agents access to physical devices in Google’s lab for testing.

Finding memory leaks with Claude

Google is also giving agents more ways to investigate problems after an app is built, including performance issues, production crashes and memory leaks. In one demo, Claude Code worked with LeakCanary, an open source leak-detection library, to check critical user journeys for memory leaks using a single instruction from the developer.

Claude Code ran the journeys across multiple devices in parallel, analyzed heap dumps through the CLI’s LeakCanary integration, and traced the leaks back to the offending code. It then made the fixes and reran the tests to confirm they worked. Google says the tooling helped capable models complete these investigations nearly twice as fast while using up to 25% fewer tokens.

autonomous bug-finding can outrun autonomous bug-fixing — an Anthropic scanner flagged some 29,000 possible vulnerabilities in open-source code while only a few hundred were ever fixed.

The demo is very impressive, and it also runs against a record that counsels patience, since autonomous bug-finding can outrun autonomous bug-fixing — an Anthropic scanner flagged some 29,000 possible vulnerabilities in open-source code while only a few hundred were ever fixed.

A companion android signals command now pipes Android vitals and Firebase Crashlytics data into the same terminal workflow, which gives agents a direct line to production crashes, ANRs, and memory problems, but none of this retires the human in the loop, as developers who watched Claude Code land a Linux kernel fix only for reviewers to catch a race condition can attest.

A companion android signals command now pipes Android vitals and Firebase Crashlytics data into the same terminal workflow

Benchmarking agents with Android Bench

Google is also introducing Android Bench 2.0 to evaluate how models and agent harnesses perform on more complex Android development tasks. It tests whether completed apps actually run with assignments ranging from building an app from mockups to migrating an existing interface. Some tasks are modeled on work that would take an Android engineer several days, and the benchmark also measures completion time and cost.

item.title: GitHub debuts Copilot Fusion, a new model selection & orchestration system that beats Claude Code for half the API cost
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
GitHub has debuted GitHub Copilot Fusion, a new system that handles model selection and orchestration for coding tasks so developers

The post GitHub debuts Copilot Fusion, a new model selection & orchestration system that beats Claude Code for half the API cost appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
GitHub has debuted GitHub Copilot Fusion, a new system that handles model selection and orchestration for coding tasks so developers don’t have to. 

Combining the advanced runtime model orchestration from Project HydraFusion with Copilot Auto Model Selection, Copilot Fusion can now handle both model selection and orchestration. GitHub says Fusion Max delivered comparable benchmark performance to Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max at about half the average API cost and in about 40% less time per task.

Generally available now, GitHub Copilot Fusion is part of GitHub’s new vision to make GitHub “the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world,” with developers delegating model choices while retaining responsibility for the direction and outcome of the work.

GitHub announced the news on Wednesday at GitHub Universe in San Francisco, the company’s flagship developer event.

GitHub Copilot Fusion is the decider now 

For tasks involving reasoning, code generation, debugging, or tool use, GitHub says developers can delegate decisions about which models to use and how they work together. Its instructions: “choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you.”

That sounds like a time-saver, since different tasks benefit from different models based on capabilities and cost. With Copilot Fusion working as the “model picker,” developers don’t have to weigh performance and price for every task.

More compelling is the idea that developers can use Copilot Fusion to strategically switch models mid-workflow, letting the system jump between models based on what best suits each step. 

After analyzing what the task requires and choosing a model, the system orchestrates the next steps based on what makes the most sense. That may be a single model doing everything, a “cascading” workflow where a quality check evaluates one model’s response and then decides to accept it or escalate it, or a “critique” workflow where one model reviews another’s work.

That could reduce the mental load for developers who may inadvertently choose inefficient models when their attention drifts.

As Hari Pokhrel, principal software engineer at AT&T, describes in a statement for GitHub: “Previously, developers would often choose a more powerful model for a complex task and forget to switch back for everyday activities.” 

So, what do developers get to decide for themselves?

Mostly, the effort level. 

While Copilot Fusion handles model selection and orchestration, developers choose the effort level: Fusion Standard for everyday coding; Fusion High for more challenging tasks and deeper reasoning; Fusion Max for the most demanding, complex work.

That’s if you’re free and comfortable letting GitHub’s systems take the lead. If you prefer, developers can implement other controls. 

Per GitHub, enterprise administrators can control which models Copilot Fusion can choose from, disabling certain models for Copilot Fusion without disabling them for the entire developer team. Administrators can also adjust the policy state for each model independently and set whether Copilot Fusion is or isn’t the default model for Copilot users.

The case for letting Copilot Fusion be your guide

According to GitHub and Pokhrel’s statement, offloading model selection and orchestration to the new fusion system is the smarter route for developers, letting you balance performance and cost without the friction of choosing between models.

GitHub says it has improved performance since launching Project HydraFusion as a research preview in September 2026. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, GitHub reports that Copilot Fusion Max scored 60, within two points of Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max. GitHub says Fusion Max delivered that result at about half the average API cost per task, using about half as many tokens and taking about 40% less time per task.

In the statement supplied to The New Stack by GitHub, Pokhrel credits Copilot Fusion Standard with improving token efficiency at AT&T, reducing unnecessary spending, and preserving capacity for higher-value work.

Model routing is becoming the default

Copilot Fusion is one piece of GitHub’s future vision, released alongside a slew of other products at the conference, including the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot Projects, and Copilot Automations.

By deferring model selection to its system, GitHub thinks developers will have more time and brainspace to focus on other work. 

It looks like everyone is moving that way. This month, Ramp described moving model selection into Open SWE, its open-source coding agent. In the summer, Replit did the same, making its “intelligent model routing” system the default across every account.

Developers pick the effort level. Copilot Fusion picks the models. An AT&T engineer say it's "improved token efficiency."

item.title: GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
GitHub is seeing unprecedented demand and is updating its core infrastructure to keep pace. In August, GitHub said it was

The post GitHub saw 7.4B commits in September, adding 4M CPU cores and 160 PB of storage to keep up appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
GitHub is seeing unprecedented demand and is updating its core infrastructure to keep pace.

In August, GitHub said it was seeing 2.9 billion commits per month, up from 1.4 billion in April. At its GitHub Universe conference on Wednesday, the company announced that it is now seeing 7.4 billion commits per month. To put that into perspective, developers pushed 65 million monthly commits to the platform in 2024.

That kind of growth is a great problem to have, but the company’s outages have become something of a recurring theme. The reason is rapid usage growth, driven mostly by “agentic demand,” as the company puts it.

4 million more CPU cores

In August, GitHub CTO Vlad Fedorov announced that the platform had added 3 million CPU cores — mostly on Azure — to support this growth. Now, GitHub says it has added 4 million CPU cores, plus 160 petabytes of high-speed storage and more compute power for GitHub Actions so far this year

The company also added 50 Tb/s of network capacity to keep all of this data flowing.

A new GitHub architecture is coming

GitHub also used this announcement to reiterate its commitment to rearchitecting its platform to separate compute and storage. It first talked about this earlier this month. At that time, the company noted that its internal benchmarks show that this new architecture can deliver up to 35x higher write throughput, for example.

“Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture,” Jay Parikh, the EVP for Core AI at Microsoft, writes in the announcement.

Separating compute and storage isn’t exactly radical in 2026, but it shows GitHub was trying to scale on a legacy foundation. Moving to Azure and its services was essentially the only option, especially as the company’s own data center was out of capacity.
