GitHub now sees 7.4 billion commits a month, driven largely by AI agents, and is adding 4 million CPU cores and rearchitecting its platform to keep up.

item.title: Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Nvidia on Wednesday launched Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, its latest multilingual transcription model. The new open-weight model, the company says, ranks

The post Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia on Wednesday launched Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, its latest multilingual transcription model. The new open-weight model, the company says, ranks first on Hugging Face’s Open ASR open model leaderboard for English, with an average word error rate of 5.33%, and also sits at the top of two speaker-attribution benchmarks.

But what’s maybe even more interesting is that this is a promptable transcription model. Being promptable here means that the user can give the model specific instructions before it listens. Typically, that means setting the context for the transcription by telling the model that a given audio file is a medical discussion in English, for example, and giving it a list of medical terms.

Users can also tell the model to label each speaker or ask it questions about the audio. They can request a verbatim transcript or a cleaned-up version, and tell it how to format numbers, for example.

Nvidia bundles these capabilities, along with translation, into a single checkpoint, which could simplify the work of building applications around them.

Ideally, setting this context reduces the error rate. The trade-off is that these models are much larger than traditional transcription models, which are often under a billion parameters in size. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 4 billion active parameters.

This isn’t a completely new concept, though. We’ve recently seen some other promptable speech-to-text models like Mistral’s Voxtral models and AssemblyAI’s Universal 3 Pro.

Nvidia, though, is able to rival Voxtral’s error rate with far fewer active parameters. On Artificial Analysis’s benchmark, Nemotron scores a 2.81% word error rate, compared with Voxtral Small’s 2.77%, while using about 4 billion active parameters versus 24 billion. That comparison measures accuracy against active parameter counts, though, rather than runtime or memory requirements.

The model can transcribe 40 languages — and translate 31 of those to or from English. Speaker attribution works for 13 of those languages, and it can distinguish between up to eight speaker voices. Audio Q&A was trained in English.

The model handles recordings up to an hour long. It’s built for recorded audio, though, and doesn’t support live streaming.

Developers can serve the model with vLLM or run it locally with NeMo-Speech.cpp. Nvidia says it runs on a single GPU, with supported hardware ranging from Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Since this is an open-weight model (under the  OpenMDW-1.1 license), users can fine-tune it to their needs in order to reduce the error rate by using NeMo Speech’s fine-tuning tools, among other tools.

In a medical transcription case study, Nvidia says fine-tuning reduced word error rate on held-out speakers from 22.44% with its best prompt to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction. The complete adaptation workflow took about 14 GPU-hours on a single GB300.

Nvidia is also releasing Granary v2, a reusable data curation pipeline built with NeMo Curator, along with public manifests covering roughly 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora. Developers can run the pipeline on their own recordings to prepare their data for customization. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.

The post Nvidia launches a promptable transcription model appeared first on The New Stack.
Nvidia’s new open-weight Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe takes instructions before it listens and tops Hugging Face’s English speech recognition leaderboard.

item.title: What happens when the agent is long gone, but its access key lives on?
item.dc:creator: Zeen Rachidi
item.description:
Imagine: There’s a line on the credential report that no one on the platform team can explain. An IAM user

The post What happens when the agent is long gone, but its access key lives on? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine: There’s a line on the credential report that no one on the platform team can explain. An IAM user called research-agent-2 has an access key created 14 months ago that was last used 11 months ago. And it’s still active. 

The project it supported closed long ago, and the person who approved it doesn’t even work at the company anymore. 

While this example is hypothetical, the lifecycle problem isn’t.

This doesn’t require carelessness. An agent is created for a task, the task ends, and nobody revisits its access. A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab. AWS IAM user access keys don’t expire automatically, so a forgotten key stays valid until somebody disables or deletes it.

“A departing person triggers offboarding; a finished agent just leaves a closed tab.”

OWASP puts improper offboarding first in its 2025 Top 10 for non-human identities, and the remedy reads like this series’ premise: retire what’s no longer needed, and give the rest an accountable owner. The hard part is knowing what exists. 

The problem is that attackers move faster than an annual audit ever could. In September 2026, GreyNoise documented an AI-orchestrated campaign against PaperCut servers: the attacker went from an empty workspace to remote code execution at a real victim in under four hours, and once launched, the campaign compromised at least eleven organizations in 26 seconds. That wasn’t an attack using abandoned AWS IAM keys. It shows how quickly exposed access becomes useful once an attacker is in, and why slow inventory and revocation are dangerous.

An agent’s access can outlive its purpose unless someone governs its lifecycle.

The last three articles covered attaching an owner at discovery, reassigning one before a last day, and what happens when the owner is an agent. Credentials add a related problem, with one distinction. An agent’s deployment identity is what authenticates it, or the deployment platform, to a cloud account. 

“A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access.”

A provisioned credential is a persistent key, secret, or token that a deployment creates for some other workload; the two have different owners and revocation procedures. A forgotten VM costs money; a forgotten credential can grant access. The remedy is still a query, a policy, and a clock, each used for the part of the problem it can solve.

1. The query that finds keys no one is using

CloudQuery can sync AWS IAM credential reports into aws_iam_credential_reports when that table is enabled in the source configuration. The report lists up to two access-key slots per user. This query, written for the ClickHouse dialect CloudQuery Platform uses, takes the latest synced row for each report, turns the slots into rows, and returns active IAM user keys that are at least 90 days old and unused for at least 90 days.

SQL
WITH latest_reports AS (
    SELECT
        _cq_platform_id,
        arn,
        `user` AS principal,
        access_key1_active,
        access_key_1_last_rotated,
        access_key_1_last_used_date,
        access_key2_active,
        access_key_2_last_rotated,
        access_key_2_last_used_date
    FROM aws_iam_credential_reports
    ORDER BY _cq_sync_group_id DESC, _cq_sync_time DESC
    LIMIT 1 BY _cq_platform_id
),
keys AS (
    SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal,
           1 AS key_slot,
           access_key1_active AS active,
           access_key_1_last_rotated AS created,
           access_key_1_last_used_date AS last_used
    FROM latest_reports
    UNION ALL
    SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal,
           2 AS key_slot,
           access_key2_active AS active,
           access_key_2_last_rotated AS created,
           access_key_2_last_used_date AS last_used
    FROM latest_reports
)
SELECT _cq_platform_id, arn, principal,
       key_slot, created, last_used
FROM keys
WHERE principal != '<root_account>'
  AND active = true
  AND created < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY
  AND (
      last_used IS NULL
      OR last_used < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY
  )
ORDER BY last_used NULLS FIRST, principal, key_slot;

The active flags, access_key1_active and access_key2_active, have no underscore before the digit; the date columns do. On Platform, a table name already points at the latest complete snapshot, so the latest-row clause matters on destinations that keep history, where it can also resurface a user deleted since. 

The 90-day window is a review threshold, not a verdict: quarterly jobs have quiet keys, and a null or placeholder last-used date means investigate, not “never needed.” The report doesn’t say which agent used an account; correlate with audit logs and a named owner. The query skips the root account, whose access keys need a separate, urgent audit; AWS recommends having none.

On PostgreSQL, quote "user" with double quotes, use interval '90 days', and replace LIMIT 1 BY with DISTINCT ON. Here the ARN, which is unique per IAM user, identifies each report:

SQL
WITH latest_reports AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (arn)
           arn, "user" AS principal,
           access_key1_active, access_key_1_last_rotated, access_key_1_last_used_date,
           access_key2_active, access_key_2_last_rotated, access_key_2_last_used_date
    FROM aws_iam_credential_reports
    ORDER BY arn, _cq_sync_time DESC
),
keys AS (
    SELECT arn, principal, 1 AS key_slot,
           access_key1_active AS active,
           access_key_1_last_rotated AS created,
           access_key_1_last_used_date AS last_used
    FROM latest_reports
    UNION ALL
    SELECT arn, principal, 2 AS key_slot,
           access_key2_active AS active,
           access_key_2_last_rotated AS created,
           access_key_2_last_used_date AS last_used
    FROM latest_reports
)
SELECT split_part(arn, ':', 5) AS account_id, arn, principal,
       key_slot, created, last_used
FROM keys
WHERE principal <> '<root_account>'
  AND active
  AND created < now() - interval '90 days'
  AND (last_used IS NULL OR last_used < now() - interval '90 days')
ORDER BY last_used NULLS FIRST, principal, key_slot;

The result is a prioritized review list. Next, the human question matters: who owns this credential, what still depends on it, and when should it stop working?

Other clouds raise the same concern elsewhere. In Entra ID, entraid_serviceprincipals includes credential metadata and entraid_serviceprincipal_owners shows who’s accountable; inspect identifiers and validity dates, not secret values, since Microsoft Graph returns secretText only at creation. In Google Cloud, gcp_iam_service_account_keys can inventory service-account keys if that table is enabled in your sync, but inventory alone doesn’t show use; check Google Cloud’s audit logs.

2. The policy that keeps agents from minting keys

The query cleans up what exists. An env zero approval policy can stop certain new keys at deploy time, but only where env zero governs the deployment: policies are enforced at deploy and destroy, not for credentials created in a console, by an external script, or by an env zero task, and they don’t revoke the identity authenticating a deployment. Cloud-native IAM controls, like an AWS service control policy or GCP’s organization policy for service account keys, and the inventory above still do that work.

Assign the policy to a project and every environment under it, subprojects included, inherits it. It doesn’t need to know whether a person or an agent clicked Deploy; it refuses selected long-lived credential types in Terraform and OpenTofu plans. Prefer federation where you can: env zero supports OIDC-based deployment authentication, and an AWS role issues temporary credentials that expire with the session, though the role itself doesn’t.

package env0

import future.keywords.contains 
import future.keywords.every 
import future.keywords.if 
import future.keywords.in

key_resources := {
	"aws_iam_access_key",
	"aws_iam_user_login_profile",
	"aws_iam_service_specific_credential",
	"aws_iam_signing_certificate",
	"google_service_account_key",
	"azuread_service_principal_password",
	"azuread_application_password",
	"azuread_service_principal_certificate",
	"azuread_application_certificate",
}

# A real Terraform or OpenTofu plan carries format_version, and omits
# resource_changes entirely when there is nothing to change.
tf_plan(p) if {
	is_object(p)
	p.format_version
}

standard_plan if {
	not input.plan.is_run_all
	tf_plan(input.plan)
}

run_all_plan if {
	input.plan.is_run_all == true
	is_object(input.plan.modules)
	count(input.plan.modules) > 0
	every _, m in input.plan.modules {
		tf_plan(m)
	}
}

resource_changes := object.get(input.plan, "resource_changes", []) if standard_plan

resource_changes := [rc |
	some _, m in input.plan.modules
	some rc in object.get(m, "resource_changes", [])
] if run_all_plan

deny contains msg if {
	not standard_plan
	not run_all_plan
	msg := "Unsupported plan format for the credential policy"
}

deny contains msg if {
	some rc in resource_changes
	key_resources[rc.type]
	"create" in rc.change.actions
	msg := sprintf("%s: long-lived credential prohibited", [rc.address])
}

allow if count(deny) == 0

The policy reads a standard Terraform or OpenTofu plan, or the module map from Terragrunt run-all. A plan with no changes can omit resource_changes, so an empty plan counts as valid, while an unrecognized shape is denied rather than silently allowed; attach it only to projects whose templates produce these formats, since Pulumi, CloudFormation, and Kubernetes deployments would all be denied. Replacements include a create action, so they’re caught. The resource list is an example, and the policy can’t see a hardcoded secret or a key generated outside Terraform.

The allow rule matters: with it, anything not denied proceeds without manual approval; without it, a policy that returns nothing defaults to pending, and every deployment waits for a person. Test with the full env zero input wrapper, not bare terraform show -json output, covering key creation, role-only plans, replacements, run-all, missing plan data, and destroys. ENV0_PRINT_POLICY_INPUT=true logs the exact input; ENV0_OPA_VERSION pins the OPA version. The policy runs on env zero’s default OPA (0.46.1) and on 1.x, which is why it uses future.keywords imports instead of import rego.v1.

If an integration genuinely needs a persistent key, don’t just create it in another project. Use a documented exception: a named owner, a specific workload, least privilege, a revocation deadline, secure storage, monitoring, and an approval record. IAM access keys can’t be tagged, so record ownership on the identity and in your credential inventory.

3. Make sure you give every key a finite lifespan

AWS doesn’t give IAM user access keys an expiration date, so the end date has to come from somewhere else. For Terraform-managed credentials, an environment TTL gives you a teardown point: put disposable credentials in the same environment as what they serve and set a TTL. But a TTL isn’t credential expiry. 

It starts a destroy, and the key disappears only if Terraform manages it and the destroy succeeds. A failed destroy, a locked environment, a manually created key, or an identity managed elsewhere leaves access behind, so verify revocation instead of trusting the countdown. TTLs can be extended or set to infinite, and TTL limits don’t bind admins. On the Free plan, once an organization passes 250 runs in a month, TTLs are destroyed; wait for the count to reset at the start of the next month (UTC), so a key can outlive its TTL by up to a month.

Govern the trust relationship and permission scope of any OIDC federation, and rotate persistent tokens in the issuing system; destroying infrastructure doesn’t revoke the caller. Terraform-managed access keys also record their secret values in state, so protect the state backend.

For keys outside any environment lifecycle, retire them under control. The credential report doesn’t include key IDs, so look those up, check last-used metadata, confirm the owner and dependency, then deactivate the specific key:

Shell
aws iam list-access-keys \
  --user-name research-agent-2

aws iam get-access-key-last-used \
  --access-key-id <key-id>

aws iam update-access-key \
  --user-name research-agent-2 \
  --access-key-id <key-id> \
  --status Inactive

Deactivation is reversible, but it isn’t harmless: a quarterly batch or disaster-recovery job can fail long after a typical release cycle. Watch for authentication errors through an observation period matched to the workload’s schedule, get owner sign-off, then delete under your change procedure, since it isn’t reversible.

env zero’s Free plan includes custom approval policies and environment TTL, with 250 runs a month and 30 active environments. CloudQuery’s Platform has a free tier, and its CLI syncs to your own Postgres. Sync the credential report, run the query, and count the rows. It’s read-only, so the worst outcome is a list you didn’t want to see.

A credential needs an end date

A resource without an owner costs money until someone notices, and an unowned credential can grant unintended access to whoever finds it. 

“An old key doesn’t need to be labeled orphaned for an attacker to use it; it only needs to be valid.”

Agents who finished last quarter’s projects won’t flag their own credentials, and the next agent to encounter one might not belong to your organization. An old key doesn’t need to be labeled orphaned for an attacker to use it; it only needs to be valid.

AI agents leave behind active IAM keys. Learn how to find unused credentials, block persistent keys, and govern non-human identities.

item.title: AI agents need to be replaceable – without losing your work
item.dc:creator: Manveer Chawla
item.description:
An agent receives approval to process a partial refund. It sends the request to a payment API, and the process

The post AI agents need to be replaceable – without losing your work appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An agent receives approval to process a partial refund. It sends the request to a payment API, and the process crashes. Maybe the payment service completed the refund. Maybe the request never went through. A replacement agent spins up and finds an operation record marked dispatched with no outcome written.

This kind of ambiguity isn’t unique to agents. Any distributed worker crashing mid-mutation faces the same problem. But a conventional worker resumes a predetermined workflow from the last checkpoint. An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own. Given the same customer request and no outcome record, it might come up with a different plan, pick different parameters, or decide to issue a new refund instead of continuing the one already approved.

“An agent does something more dangerous: it reasons on its own.”

If the original refund went through, a second attempt refunds the customer twice. The charge still has enough remaining balance to cover another partial refund, so nothing stops it.

The replacement must inherit the original operation, not reinterpret it.

The operation must outlive the agent

An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context: all disposable. The business operation is not. The refund, its approval, its parameters, its current status. A long-running agent can preserve useful state for as long as it runs. The requirement: no essential operation should depend on the original execution surviving.

Before dispatching the refund, the application commits a durable operation record to a transactional store. That record includes the approved amount, the applicable authorization, the idempotency key the application sends to the payment provider, the application’s operation identifier in the provider’s metadata, and a status.

“An agent’s process, its in-memory variables, its transient reasoning context: all disposable. The business operation is not.”

The status moves from created to dispatched as the request leaves, and to confirmed or failed only on a provider response. If the agent crashes, the replacement retrieves this record and its correlation identifiers. A record stuck in dispatched indicates a call was attempted, but the outcome was never written.

The replacement inherits the approved operation rather than regenerating it.

When the replacement needs to verify the outcome, it can list refunds against the original charge and match the operation identifier in the returned metadata.

But the durable record isn’t just context for the replacement. The application enforces it at the tool boundary: the dispatch layer validates every outbound request against the committed record. The agent can propose a next step, but only authorized operations with their original parameters and identity reach the provider. The model can’t redefine what was approved.

ClickHouse Managed Postgres holds the business data, including the authoritative operation record that defines what the replacement is allowed to do. Native CDC replicates that data into ClickHouse. Application telemetry ships to ClickStack and agent traces to Langfuse, both configured to use the same ClickHouse service as their backend database.

Because business data, application telemetry, and agent traces land in one database, tying an operation to the agent run that dispatched it and the failed HTTP call is a single-identifier query. Not a reconciliation across three tools.

Two conditions. The application has to propagate that identifier. The operation ID must appear in the Postgres row, in the Langfuse trace attributes, and in the service’s log context, because nothing correlates it for you. And the replacement reads the record from Postgres, not from the replicated copy. CDC runs with seconds of latency. The authoritative row is the one the tool boundary enforces.

Restarting execution isn’t safely resuming work

Durable execution frameworks like LangGraph and Temporal record execution progress and resume after a failure. Both recommend making side effects idempotent, because resuming doesn’t resolve one. If the refund completed while the step was still pending, the framework can restart the agent, but it can’t tell the replacement whether the payment provider committed the original request.

The durable operation record implements that idempotency guidance for an agent whose next step isn’t predetermined.

The idempotency key from the durable record connects the replacement to the original request. If the replacement retries with the same key, the provider can recognize the same operation rather than processing an independent refund. This holds even if the original agent’s in-flight request completed after the crash, or a worker assumed dead has resumed. AWS’s Builders’ Library formalizes this pattern: a caller-provided identifier recorded atomically with the mutation.

But retrying isn’t always safe. The outcome might stay unclear. Stripe documents that a 500 response on a mutation can still produce external effects. When the outcome is unknown, the replacement needs evidence to investigate.

Langfuse can show the previous agent’s tool invocation: a refund request dispatched with the recorded idempotency key. ClickStack can fill in the operational side: an outbound HTTP request to the payment service followed by a connection failure, narrowing the failure window. 

Both are available to the replacement directly. The Langfuse MCP server lets it query the previous agent’s trace by operation ID, and the ClickStack MCP server lets it search service events in the same window. Give the replacement the read tools only. It can narrow down what happened, but the tool boundary still controls what the replacement can do.

Neither trace proves the provider committed the refund. And an absent trace doesn’t prove the request was never sent, since Langfuse transmits traces asynchronously and a crash can prevent delivery. The payment provider remains the system of record for the external outcome. Execution telemetry narrows the investigation. It doesn’t replace authoritative confirmation.

Continue the work; don’t start over

The replacement has the durable record and, where the outcome was unclear, the execution evidence. Now it needs to act, but not by re-deciding what to do.

The replacement follows the recovery protocol the application defines, not its own judgment about the customer’s situation.

If the provider confirms the refund is complete, the replacement records the outcome and moves on. If the provider shows the refund is still pending or in progress, the replacement waits. Retrying would risk a duplicate. If the refund definitively failed with no external effect, the replacement revalidates preconditions before a new authorized attempt. If the outcome remains unclear, it escalates rather than guessing. A missing provider record doesn’t prove the refund was never processed. The provider may not have finalized the transaction.

“A stored approval is historical evidence, not current authority to act.”

Even after establishing the external outcome, the replacement has to verify that the world hasn’t changed. The refundable balance may have shifted. A human representative might have processed a separate refund through a different interface. The customer’s account status may have changed. Someone may have revoked the original authorization.

A stored approval is historical evidence, not current authority to act.

The real engineering question is whether a new agent can establish the work’s current objective, outstanding obligations, and uncertain effects, then continue safely without treating the predecessor’s recollections as authority.

The agent is disposable. The work isn’t.

When AI agents crash mid-task, durable records and tool boundaries ensure replacements resume work safely without duplicate actions.

item.title: From human clicks to agentic velocity: What OpenAI’s 1.2 billion scale means for your auth
item.dc:creator: Damon Tepe
item.description:
When OpenAI announced at DevDay that ChatGPT had crossed 1.2 billion weekly active users (WAUs), roughly 15% of the human

The post From human clicks to agentic velocity: What OpenAI’s 1.2 billion scale means for your auth appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When OpenAI announced at DevDay that ChatGPT had crossed 1.2 billion weekly active users (WAUs), roughly 15% of the human population, most engineering discussions naturally centered on model context windows, compute clusters, and distributed GPU inference.

However, behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale.

“Behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale.”

Before OpenAI can serve a token from an LLM, its backend systems must authenticate the request, validate OAuth2 access tokens, inspect fine-grained permissions, and maintain secure session contexts globally. To manage this massive transaction volume without introducing latency bottlenecks, OpenAI turned to Ory, utilizing its lightweight, decoupled authentication engine and OAuth2/OIDC infrastructure.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how identity scale shifts when moving from human traffic to agent workloads, why legacy IAM platforms break at this volume, and how decoupled, edge-ready authorization handles extreme throughput.

The scale problem: human traffic vs. agentic workloads

To understand why traditional IAM platforms fail at extreme scale, consider how user authentication patterns change as architectures evolve from standard web applications to agentic AI platforms. 

“When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents… the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly.”

When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents (e.g., OpenAI’s Work and Codex suites), the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly:

  1. Transaction velocity: A single user request to an AI agent can trigger dozens of downstream sub-tasks, database queries, and third-party API tool calls. Each step requires session verification and token introspection.
  2. Token introspection overhead: Legacy central identity providers (IdPs) typically validate access tokens via centralized RPCs or database lookups. At billions of requests per minute, centralized introspection introduces severe network hops and database lock contention.
  3. Stateless edge verification: To prevent authorization from becoming the primary bottleneck in the request path, session validation must happen synchronously at the edge using lightweight cryptographic verification (such as JSON Web Key Sets / JWKS caching) rather than stateful network calls.

Architectural comparison: modern composable IAM vs. legacy monolithic SaaS

When evaluating identity platforms for ultra-high throughput, engineering teams frequently hit performance and cost walls with traditional multi-tenant identity SaaS products (e.g., Auth0, Okta, Ping Identity).

“OpenAI wanted a partner that could help enable our vision for owning our identity processes, data, and success. We have a lot of partners, and Ory is one of our best.”

  • Benjamin Billings,  Engineering Manager, OpenAI (Case study)

Key infrastructure requirements for billion-user identity systems

Securing identity at scale requires a clear separation of concerns across the auth stack. Based on high-throughput deployments like OpenAI’s, modern identity architectures depend on four core principles:

1. Separation of identity state from business logic

Monolithic frameworks often bind user profiles, authentication state, and business roles together in single relational databases. High-throughput architectures decouple these responsibilities into distinct microservices:

  • Identity storage & auth engines: Dedicated microservices handling identity lifecycle, credential hashing, and session management (e.g., Ory Kratos).
  • OAuth2 / OIDC token issuance: High-performance OAuth2 server implementations capable of issuing signed access tokens and managing grant flows with minimal latency (e.g., Ory Hydra).
  • Fine-grained access control (FGAC): Relationship-based access control engines based on Google’s Zanzibar model (e.g., Ory Keto) to evaluate tuple relationships (ObjectRelationSubject) in sub-millisecond execution times.

2. Distributed persistence across cloud regions

To support global edge routing, the underlying storage layer must support geo-distributed writes and low-latency local reads. Combining a self-hosted identity engine with distributed SQL engines (such as CockroachDB or cloud-native multi-region databases) ensures token-verification state can be replicated globally without split-brain risks or cross-continental network latency.

3. Agent security: transitioning from “enforce first” to “observe mode”

As enterprises deploy autonomous agents that execute commands on users’ behalf, writing restrictive IAM policies immediately can break workflows or cause silent failures. Modern security practices emphasize runtime observability before strict policy enforcement:

  • Step 1: agent fingerprinting: Map every machine-to-machine (M2M) credential and agent service account operating across internal networks.
  • Step 2: execution tracing: Audit tool usage, API invocations, and database queries initiated by autonomous runtimes.
  • Step 3: identity delegation: Implement scoped OAuth2 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) to ensure agents operate under strict downscoped permissions tied directly to the delegating human user.

For a limited time, you can create a complimentary Ory account and turn on observe mode to learn how best to build enforcement.

“Scaling authentication to 1.2 billion weekly active users proves that identity is no longer just a security checkbox; it is a core distributed systems challenge.”

Scaling authentication to 1.2 billion weekly active users proves that identity is no longer just a security checkbox; it is a core distributed systems challenge.

As software shifts from human-driven UI interactions to high-velocity AI agent execution, engineering teams must evaluate whether their identity stack can handle exponential API volume. Decoupled, stateless-first identity engines offer the low latency, data sovereignty, and predictability modern platforms need to scale into the agentic era.

item.title: Google built AI agents a world to practice in. The physics still aren’t quite right.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4 on Tuesday, a world model that renders interactive environments in real time with simulated physics,

The post Google built AI agents a world to practice in. The physics still aren’t quite right. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4 on Tuesday, a world model that renders interactive environments in real time with simulated physics, human motion, and native audio. The photorealistic demos are seriously impressive, but arguably the real draw for anyone building AI agents is that Genie 4 gives them somewhere to run multi-step tasks before it counts.

Tejas Kulkarni, a research director at Google DeepMind, describes the approach at a press briefing as a move toward “these hybrid world models,” with Gemini writing the code and text and Genie turning it into a running scene. It gives developers a way to generate test environments on demand, although how closely those simulations reflect real-world conditions remains an open question about reliability.

It gives developers a way to generate test environments on demand.

How Gemini steers Genie 4

Genie 4 uses several Gemini models to keep its simulations running. Gemini Omni helps shape the environment, while Gemini 3.8 Flash follows what’s happening, plans the next steps and adjusts when something changes.

Instead of producing a finished video, Genie 4 lets users interact with the world as it’s generated. They can move through it with a keyboard, change the camera angle or use text prompts to alter the environment without restarting the simulation.

Instead of producing a finished video, Genie 4 lets users interact with the world as it’s generated.

Rehearsing robots in simulation

Google’s clearest example puts Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid through a game of checkers, with Gemini 4 Argon planning each move and Genie 4 rendering the results as captions steer the scene.

The company is also exploring how the technology could support its Gemini Robotics research, which gives developers the ability to test agents in changing environments without having to rebuild each simulation from scratch.

Where the physics breaks down

The catch is that Genie 4 can’t always keep those environments consistent. Objects can shift position or behave unpredictably during longer sessions, and Google acknowledges that the physics isn’t always accurate.

That complicates agent evaluations, particularly when tasks involve remembering locations or returning to earlier states. A failed run could reflect a problem with the agent or the simulation itself, and Google hasn’t demonstrated that Genie 4 can replace traditional physics engines in high-stakes testing.

Game developers are using Genie 4 to explore prototypes and test game mechanics before writing engine code, while enterprise partners are looking at ways to generate their own testing scenarios.

The company hasn’t published benchmarks showing how Genie 4 performs across repeated agent tests.

The company hasn’t published benchmarks showing how Genie 4 performs across repeated agent tests. This includes whether the same prompt produces consistent results, leaving leaves developers with little to go on when deciding whether to use it in automated testing.

Who gets Genie 4 access

For now, only trusted testers have access. Google plans to expand availability to Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie and select partners through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. There’s no word yet on pricing, a wider release or performance guarantees.

Google DeepMind’s Genie 4 world model lets AI agents practice multi-step tasks in generated worlds, but shaky physics limits how much to trust it.

item.title: Replit’s CEO says an idea from 1937 could make the org chart obsolete
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has spent the past year watching AI agents absorb the routine execution inside his

The post Replit’s CEO says an idea from 1937 could make the org chart obsolete appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has spent the past year watching AI agents absorb the routine execution inside his own company, and in a thread posted to X on Monday, he argues the same shift is bearing down on everyone else, with businesses moving toward a self-driving company where, in his words, “humans exercise judgment and agents execute most of the work.”

He rests the case on Ronald Coase’s 1937 question of why firms exist in the first place, the economist’s answer being that companies survive because coordinating work inside them beats coordinating it through open markets, and he contends AI agents are about to collapse the internal coordination costs — the management, the meetings, the reporting — that firms have swallowed as fixed for nearly a century.

In the thread, Masad posted, “The Rise of the Self-Driving Company,” in which he writes that “every company in the Fortune 500 will be a Self-Driving Company” by the end of 2030.

“Every company in the Fortune 500 will be a Self-Driving Company” by the end of 2030.

What the Agent Habitat is

Replit is moving toward that vision with Replit for Business, which gives AI agents access to company systems, data, and workflows while keeping permissions and approvals in place.

Masad calls the underlying concept the “Agent Habitat,” a space where agents can work with employees and one another without having unrestricted access to company resources. It’s still more of a blueprint; Replit has not yet published a full technical specification explaining how those controls would work together.

Why agent sprawl is risky

Masad is trying to solve a rising problem as companies deploy more AI agents. Many still operate through scattered chat windows, personal accounts, and custom scripts, often with whatever credentials and data employees give them. Companies have little visibility into what those agents can access or what they’ve done.

Giving agents more freedom might not be the answer, either. Recent research shows how easily coding agents can overstep their intended scope, even when doing legitimate work.

Replit’s Agent Habitat aims to strike a balance by giving agents access to the tools and data they need while enforcing permissions.

Replit’s Agent Habitat aims to strike a balance by giving agents access to the tools and data they need while enforcing permissions. Masad also wants companies to benefit from what their agents learn. If an employee corrects an agent, that feedback could become part of the instructions other agents follow. One team could reuse a workflow across the company rather than building it from scratch.

Keeping humans in control

On Tuesday, Replit moved closer to that vision with Cloud Agents, which let employees change a company’s codebase without setting up a development environment or needing to know how the application works behind the scenes.

Engineers still have the final say over what ships, but employees can bring them tested changes instead of waiting for someone to pick up a ticket.

Replit also lets administrators set up shared development environments, so employees don’t have to configure repositories, database, and services themselves. Credentials are managed centrally rather than distributed across teams, reflecting a trend that shifts away from long-lived credentials.

Cloud Agents and code reviews

The company is also experimenting with agents learning from code reviews. When an engineer flags a problem, Cloud Agents can suggest updates to the team’s shared instructions, called “skills,” so future agents can avoid making the same mistake. Engineers must approve those updates, and the feature remains in early access.

Replit says the shared instructions are already helping reduce costs. In its own testing, the company reported a 51% drop in token consumption and said a routine data task that previously took 16 minutes could be completed in one, without sacrificing output quality. That’s a notable improvement, especially since recent research has shown how much an agent’s performance depends on its harness and how it handles memory.

The company has also seen gains in its own engineering teams, where code output nearly tripled during the first half of 2026 without longer review times or an increase in reversions or production incidents. Agents are now being used beyond engineering, with designers building features, and support teams investigating customer issues.

Agents are now being used beyond engineering, with designers building features, and support teams investigating customer issues.

There are limits to those numbers. Replit hasn’t shared enough detail to independently verify the gains or separate the impact of agents from other changes to how its teams work. What works at an AI-native company like Replit could also be much harder to pull off at a large enterprise with decades of existing systems and processes.

Cloud Agents are now generally available to Pro and Enterprise customers, while skills remain in early access. The broader Agent Habitat vision is still taking shape, and Replit hasn’t yet demonstrated that agents can handle the kind of company-wide work Masad describes.

Replit CEO Amjad Masad wants AI agents to run companies by 2030. His Agent Habitat and new Cloud Agents are the first steps toward that bet.

item.title: “The panic hasn’t turned into patching”: What security researchers really think about the PHP2Shell response
item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.description:
The PHP panic has not turned to patching: And that’s bad news, capital B, as PHP2Shell attacks ramp up. We

The post “The panic hasn’t turned into patching”: What security researchers really think about the PHP2Shell response appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
The PHP panic has not turned to patching: And that’s bad news, capital B, as PHP2Shell attacks ramp up.

We know the paired PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, aka PHP2Shell, have a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score of 9.2, which is scary bad. After all, about 70% of websites with an identifiable server-side language run on PHP-based systems like WordPress.

But does that mean people are patching their servers as fast as they can?

To quote Moshe Siman Tov Bustan of Ox security: “The panic hasn’t turned into patching.” Ox reports in a new blog post that of October 26, five days after disclosure, the picture has barely shifted – 93.6% still exposed.“

Wow! Ow!

“…remediation isn’t in panic state, it barely crawls, with more headlines than fixed instances in the wild”

Bustan goes on to write, “Remediation is too slow, while everyone panics about PHP CVEs, remediation isn’t in panic state, it barely crawls, with more headlines than fixed instances in the wild… we missed the opportunity to actually get our patches out the door – and now, when exploits are out there, proven in the wild and not just speculation – we’ve left our most precious assets exposed for the next hacker to take advantage of.”

We really do like living dangerously, don’t we? 

It’s not just Ox reporting abysmal PHP2Shell patch numbers. Censys, a security company, in its PHP2Shell survey as of Tuesday, reports that about 11.2 million Internet-facing PHP services are reporting patched versions. That’s not as impressive as it sounds. These counts are based on the PHP versions servers report, and because Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, some “vulnerable” services may already be patched.

Some 32.5 million are still showing they’re running unsafe PHP versions. Censys also doesn’t know what 61,303,506 PHP services (58% of all detected) are running. Many of these are likely to be running unsupported versions of PHP.
